What are the rules, and what is the difference which is proposed to be adjusted ?

(Translation.) In answer to the hon. leader of the opposition, I may say that the regulations governing the notices required by parliament in connection with private Bills are no longer what they should he. The Committee on Standing Orders, on examining the notices given in the newspapers
regarding private Bills, came to the conclusion that the rule in this regard should be amended. For instance, the committee are of opinion that it is unnecessary to have these notices given for such a long period of time. Moreover, they found out that a difficulty arose in the case of a railway or any company whose business extended over more than one district. In accordance with the regulation now in force, notices should appear in every county in each district, while the committee think it would be sufficient to issue such notices in one only. This same difficulty arose formerly, and a similar committee was appointed. It is for the purpose of definitely settling this matter that it is proposed to appoint the committee referred to in the motion.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 200) respecting inspection and sale of seeds.
Will the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fisher) he good enough to state briefly the purport of the Bill ?

The Bill is for the purpose of trying to remedy some defects, and I might almost say grievances, in connection with the sale of agricultural seeds. In consequence of complaints and facts that came to the knowledge of the department some two years ago the department has been carrying on a good deal of investigation into the business of the sale of agricultural seeds, especially in this country. A condition of affairs was found which showed that there is a great deal of seed sold which is not full value for what is paid for it, and the people who purchase it in many instances are-I will not say imposed upon, perhaps, because I do not think for a moment that there is any intention or desire to commit fraud-hut from ignorance and carelessness are not getting what they think they are getting. I believe that the evil has reached a magnitude in this country that requires a certain amount of regulation, and it is the purpose of this Bill to provide for such regulation. When the Bill is printed and before hon. members, it will be, perhaps, more suitable and convenient for me to go into the details more fully than at the present time.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

subtopic: MONTREAL HARBOUR-ADVANCES TO THE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.

speechtext:
House went in committee on the following proposed resolution.
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide as follows :-
1.	The Governor in Council may from time to time advance and pay to the corporation of the Harbour Commissioners of'Montreal (hereinafter called ' the corporation '), in addition to the moneys authorized to be advanced to the corporation by the Governor in Council by chapter 10 of the statutes of 1896 (first session), and by chapter 47 of the statutes of 1898, and by chapter 9 of the statutes of 1901, such sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of three million dollars, as are required to enable the corporation to construct such further terminal facilities as are necessary properly to equip the port of Montreal.
2.	No such advances shall be made unless the plans, specifications and estimates for the works to be performed by the corporation, and on which the money so to be advanced is to be expended, have first been submitted to and approved by the Governor in Council.
3.	The corporation shall, upon any advance being made, deposit with the Minister of Finance and Receiver General debentures of the corporation equal to par value to the advance so made (which debentures the corporation are hereby authorized to issue), and such debentures so issued shall be of such amounts as the
Minister of Finance and Receiver General determines, and shall bear date on the day when such advance is made, and shall be repayable within twenty-five years from the date of their issue, and in the meantime shall bear interest at the rate of three per cent per annum, such interest to be payable half yearly on the first day of July and the first day of January in each year.
4.	The principal and interest of the sums advanced under the authority of this Act to the corporation shall be paid by the corporation out of its revenue mentioned in section 8 of chapter 10 of the statutes of 1896 (first session), and shall be a charge upon the said revenue in the same manner and to the same extent as if the sums so advanced had been borrowed by the corporation under the said chapter 10.-The Minister of Finance.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W.
S.	Fielding). With the increasing and very rapid growth of the trade of the country, there has arisen necessity for better means of transportation and -better terminal facilities at our ports, especially at the port of Montreal, which handles such a very large proportion of the total trade of the country. We have been aiding the port of Montreal during recent years by granting loans to the Harbour Commissioners to enable them to provide the necessary facilities. Going back as far as the year 1896, provision was made for a loan of $2,000,000 which was intended not only to deal with works which were then in hand but also to pay off some existing indebtedness. In 1898 provision was made for a further advance to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal of $2,000,000. and in the year 1901, a further advance of $1,000,000. So that by these three separate Acts of 1896, 1898 and 1901 authority was taken for the advance from time to time of sums aggregating $5,000,000. A portion of this was advanced at three and a half per cent, but the latter portion at three per cent. The advances made by the government under the authority of these Acts, up to a recent date, amount to $3,450,000- $2,000,000 of this was advanced under the earlier Acts at three and a half per cent and $1,450,000 under the later Acts at three per cent. Therefore there would be a balance available to the commissioners at present out of existing authorized loans of $1,550,000. Against that, however, the commissioners have entered into certain contracts and have works in contemplation which it is understood will absorb nearly all that sum, leaving about $294,000 which they have not applied to any work already authorized. Under the legislation now proposed, the commissioners will have available this sum of $294,000 out of the past advances, over and above their present contracts, and $3,000,000 under the proposed resolution now- before the committee. The purposes to which it is contemplated to apply this money as stated by the commissioners is as follows :

There will, I am sure, be no question on the part of the House as to the readiness of the government and parliament to afford all reasonable assistance to provide these facilities at the great port of Montreal. Perhaps, I should say, although it is hardly necessary, that the interest of these loans in the past has in all cases been promptly met by the Montreal Harbour Commissioners. They have from time to time met their obligations and they represent to ns now that with the growing business of the port they will be able to meet tlie larger obligations which this resolution creates. As X have pointed out. two-thirds of this proposed loan, over $2,000,000, is to be applied to the construction of steel sheds, and they estimate that these sheds will yield a rental which will amply compensate them and enable them to provide the interest. They also represent that as respects the balance of the indebtedness the Increasing business Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
of Montreal will enable them to provide for it as they have done so promptly in the post. The trade which passes over the wharfs in Montreal is of course not the trade of Montreal Itself but the trade of the whole Dominion, and the charges that are levied upon it have in the past enabled the commissioners to obtain a liberal revenue and to meet all their obligations. They are satisfied that with the increased business of the country they will continue to meet these obligations. The government, feeling satisfied that these representations are well founded, and that the object is one in which the House will readily concur, have brought forward this resolution asking that a further sum of $3,000,000 may he advanced to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal for the purposes stated and on the same terms and conditions as the grants of former years.

There is no doubt that we canuot stand still in providing facilities for the port of Montreal, but that we must continue the improvements begun there, and these improvements, before they are finished, will cost a very considerable amount. I doubt very much, in spite of the details which the hon. minister has given us, whether it will be possible, with the sum of $3,000,000, to carry out these improvements to the very end.
But what I wish to call the attention of the government and of the committee to is the fact that we have adopted with respect to the port of Montreal a very singular policy. We are accumulating upou that unfortunate port an immense indebtedness; and the harbour commissioners, as the hou. minister has stated, have always been ready to meet their obligations when they have become due. I calculate that when this sum of $3,000,000 has been raised for the port of Montreal, that port will be indebted in the sum of $10,222,000, upon which it is impossible to conceive, if we are to make a success of that port, that the harbour commissioners shall be able to pay the interest, without reference to the considerable sum required every year for maintenance. If we are to meet that indebtedness and to maintain the port after we have finished it, we shall have to place charges against the port which will render it anything but a free port, and place it on a footing of inferiority to all the other ports on the continent of North America. The interest on that sum of $10,222,000, when we shall have spent it-and we must move for the spending of the $3,000,000 now being loaned without delay-will amount to $351,000 a year.
Let us look at the position of that port in the last three or four years. In 1901 the indebtedness of the port of Montreal tor improvements, partly from loans advanced by the government, and partly from advances obtained otherwise, amounted to $4,372,000, bearing', I think, about 3J per

cent. The annual interest charge was $176,032, and we paid for maintenance and repairs, $12S,375; making a total expenditure in that year of $305,207; and our revenue was only $270,411. So that in the year 1901, even with this comparatively small indebtedness, we had a deficit of over $34,000. To-day the indebtedness of the port of Montreal amounts to $5,672,000, and we still have power to borrow, if I am not mistaken, $1,550,000. That is to say, at the present moment the borrowing power of the harbour commissioners amounts to $7,222,000. I have stated that I do not think, from my limited experience, though from close observation, that it is possible, even with this $3,000,000 referred to by the minister, and with the balance mentioned, for the port of Montreal to be fully equipped, as it was intended to be equipped, with all modern conveniences. I fix upon $12,000,000 rather than $10,222,000 as the amount which the port will have to incur in the way of debt before it can be equipped with modern improvements; and this would represent an annual interest charge on the port of $400,000.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is possible for the port of Montreal to meet that charge. It would cease absolutely to be a free port. Revenue would have to be gathered everywhere, in every imaginable way, and even then, unless the charges were absolutely exorbitant, we could not possibly raise that sum of $400,000 a year to pay interest on this indebtedness.
What I wish to call the government's attention to is this, that it seems to me we are proceeding otherwise with Montreal than we ought to do, and otherwise than we are proceeding with everything else connected with the transportation system. We have given a large amount of money to railways in the west. We have equipped or we are equipping ports on the great lakes at considerable expense. It has been admitted in the House that that equipment is necessary, and that we must be prepared to compete with our American neighbours in that respect. We have spent millions in improving the St. Lawrence route, so as to enable the commerce of the west to find an exit through that route; and recently we have taken off the canal tolls. Our object ought to be, with the advantages which nature has given us. to make transportation as easy and as cheap as possible, and to provide ports for ocean going vessels. It has been said, and I think with a great deal of truth, that we are not in a position to handle in the port of Montreal the freight from the west which nature intended we should receive, even if we had that freight. It has been said time and again that if we had a great inflow of grain into the port of Montreal, that port would be choked in a short space of time. So that it seems to me that the disposition of the government, however generous it may be, to lend money to the 140
harbour commissioners for the equipment of that port, is contrary to sound policy. I cannot repeat it too often, that we ought, starting from the west, to have a policy of transportation clearly expressed by the government. We voted yesterday a very large amount of money for a railway in the west, and hon. members will notice that we had no declaration from the government, although it was insistently called for by the leader of the opposition, as to what link in the chain or scheme of transportation that railway was going to supply; and I have never heard, since I have had the advantage of sitting in this House, any clear declaration of policy in regard to transportation from this government. The reason is that it is impossible for the government to arrive at a clear, economic conclusion with regard to this great question, which interests us so much, without incurring the displeasure or disfavour of certain localities in this country. And yet, if there is a question perhaps more important than the question of protection, which has been so much discussed lately in this House, it is this question of transportation; and, strange to say, whereas everywhere else expense is incurred by the government with the object no doubt, of furthering in some way the attainment of that great national aim, when you come to the port of Montreal, you proceed upon a method which must inevitably it seems to me, lead to difficulty.
Unless at a future day the government is prepared to abandon its claim on the harbour commissioners, it seems to me that the bankruptcy of that port will be inevitable or the commissioners will have to impose charges on the shipping and thus take away from that port its national and free character. It is not merely the port of Montreal that is concerned. Our transportation system begins in the extreme west and ends on the continent of Europe. It has several stages. The stage represented by an ocean port is not confined to the port of Montreal. There is the important port of Quebec lower down, and if we are to have a winter port, then we must find that port on the coast and be prepared to equip it as we now find it necessary to equip the port of Montreal. It is therefore no sectional question I am raising, but the question of transportation in one of its phases and I venture to say that if we are to be saddled with this additional indebtedness, we will never be able to meet the interest and will have to go into bankruptcy. It seems to me therefore that it would be better for this government to, make up its mind now as to the character to be given the port of Montreal, and if it should cost us $10,000,000 or $15,000,000, or even, as the equipment of many ports elsewhere have cost, $20,000,000 or $25,000,000, we should be prepared to incur that expense in order that the important obligations we are about to undertake with respect to railways for



tlie purpose of bringing freight from the west may prove fruitful aud give to this country all the benefits we are entitled to expect from the investment. It seems to me that the government is lacking in frankness. It seems to me that it would be better for the government, instead of spending vast sums on wharfs in divers section's of the country, to concentrate its efforts on one, two or three ports, and place them in such a position as to be able, without making any charge to handle the very considerable amount of freight which must come from the west unless our expectations should be sadly disappointed.

I am afraid that the suggestion of my hon. friend that we should abandon expenditure on wharfs elsewhere and concentrate all our expenditure in that connection on the port of Montreal is not one which would meet with general favour in this House. The alarm of my hon. friend regarding the bankruptcy of the Montreal Harbour Commissioners is not at al'l shared by the commissioners themselves. His suggestion is that these sums, which we are providing by way of a loan, should be presented as a free gift, and that the services which, under this scheme, will receive some compensation by way of a tax on the trade, shall be performed free. Let us see what these services are. About $1,000,000 of the loan will go into an elevator. Now elevator services are not free elsewhere: why should they be free in Montreal ? Elsewhere elevators charge a reasonable compensation when service is rendered.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: Are they not free in St. John and Halifax, or so low that there is not much revenue ?

I do not think that elevator services are given anywhere free. There are cases where a railway has an elevator on its line, and the elevator charge is included in the freight, but in all cases elevators are recognized as public utilities which may reasonably charge some compensation for the services they render. I do not think it would be wrong to say that a reasonable tax should be paid on grain for elevator service in Montreal. $2,000,000 out of the $3,000,000 are to be expended in building warehouses in Montreal, which is a very proper and necessary service in the handling of traffic. But we do not generally find warehouses supplied free elsewhere. Why should they be supplied free in Montreal ?
Because they are simply sheds.

A shed that costs $2,000,000 is a very respectable kind of warehouse. The harbour commissioners do not share my hon. friend's alarm. They recognize that if they own a two million dollar warehouse, it is not unreasonable Mr. MONK.
to ask the people who use it to pay a small charge, and they are satisfied that out of this small charge they will be able to pay the interest on the cost. They are satisfied that if these sheds, which are to cost over $2,000,000, be rented on terms which would not impose any undue burden on the trade, they will yield a sufficient return to enable the commissioners to pay the interest on their cost. If those who use warehouses elsewhere have to pay rent, why should they not have to pay rent when they use warehouses in Montreal ? My hon. friend will find on reflection that, in his praiseworthy desire to advance the interests of the great city in which he lives, he is a bit unreasonable. The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, who have given this matter their careful attention, are satisfied that, with the increasing trade of the country, they will be able to meet the interest. The government, in advancing the money at the low rate of 3 per cent, is certainly doing something which, I am sure, will be appreciated, but unless it can be shown that charges, such as rentals for the use of these warehouses and of elevators, are excessive, my hon. friend has not much of a case. I do not think that the people of Montreal will be so unreasonable as to expect to be provided with free warehouses and eleva tors. In advancing this money at a low rate of interest this government and parliament are following out the policy which originated with our predecessors, and in my opinion the people of Montreal will be less alarmed than my hon. friend and more willing to recognize the liberal manner in which we are dealing with that great port.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext: The question raised by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has a wider scope than the hon. Minister of Finance seems to imagine. It is not a Montreal question. I have no doubt that my hon. friend knows that last year the trade in the port of Montreal, export and import, reached the very large amount of $191,000,-000-nearly half the trade of the whole country.
Not nearly half, but thirty-five per cent.

Well, let us say thirty-five per cent. But that in itself is a pretty large amount of money. My hon. friend, if he allows me to say so in all deference, takes a narrow view of the situation. He tells us that we must not expect that Montreal shall have free harbour accommodation. It is not Montreal that is asking that, but the trade of the country. Why did my hon. friend a few weeks ago, consent to have free canals this year ? For the very excellent reason that he wished to help in developing trade through Canadian channels. The government holds the Canadian system of canals on which we have spent about I $70,000,000. We are further equipping the

entrance to the canals at federal expense ; we are equipping, at federal expense our harbours on the lakes. We have not done enough. Let us do more. But why, I ask, does the Minister of Finance wish to put a stop to the trade at Montreal ?-for that is what it means. Raising a loan means paying the interest on that loan. X am sure that my hon. friend from .Taeques Cartier (Mr. Monk) did not intend to convey the idea that the harbour commissioners of Montreal were going into bankruptcy. There is no fear of that; but there is fear, and well-founded fear, that if we go on piling up debts upon the port of Montreal the trade will go elsewhere. I believe that my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier is perfectly right when he says that Montreal is treated as no other port in the country is treated. The port of Quebec started borrowing money ; the trade did not materialize ; the interest is not being paid, and the port of Quebec cannot pay it. I do not blame them for not paying the interest- the trade does not afford the means of paying the interest. I would be perfectly ready to spend more money in Quebec, if it were necessary. But I say that it is a narrow policy-and I say it in no offensive manner- to raise a wall against the trade of Montreal both import and export. But that Is Just what the Minister of Finance is doing now. He has mentioned the harbour board. I happen to have had long and frequent intercourse with that body ; and I know that, this year, the harbour commissioners were anxious not to borrow any more. But they have been informed, officially or unofficially, that they could not succeed in getting money. I have been told by several of them that that is the reason they have been obliged to accept a loan. I believe they are making a mistake. I have said it elsewhere, and I say here, that they should not have made a loan-they should not have consented to do so. Had they taken this position the government would have been responsible for the refusal to equip the port at federal expense as it ought to do. not in the interest of Montreal, but in the interest of the country at large. Now, there is no use in making long speeches ; it is a very clear question. Are we going to have Canadian trade through Canadian channels? If that is what we want, let us take the means to bring it about, and one of the means necessary is to make our ports as free as possible. I agree with the Minister of Finance that we must not expect to have free elevators, to have free wharfage. But my hon. friend must not lose sight of one thing, and that Is that, besides the interest on debts incurred, there is a very large expenditure of money for maintenance. It will always be necessary to raise money for that purpose. In my humble opinion, the government should assume the port of Montreal and deal with it as a great national problem, just as we deal with our great system of canals. Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax 140$	s
should be national harbours. In point of fact we have dealt with several of them- with all of them-partially in that way.
Not all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No, I said partially- that is the word I used.
But what the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) said was that we had dealt with all of them partially as national harbours. I take exception to that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Blair) say what exception he takes ?

I take exception to that as applied to the port of St. John. All that the government has done at the port of St. John is to furnish railway accommodation. In the way of constructing piers and wharfs, it has done nothing whatever.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Unless my eyes have greatly deceived me, I have seen at the port of St. John wharfs
For railway purposes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Oh, well, my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Blair) is drawing a red herring across the trail. And a very poor herring it is. Why my hon. friend himself has spent over $2,000,000 in St. John on wharf accommodation, shed accommodation and elevator accommodation. And he has done more than that, he has spent in Halifax a large amount of money in providing accommodation for which there is no trade. The elevator of Halifax costs this country a large amount of money every year. There is no trade for it. When it was built, we knew very well that there would not be much trade for it. I consented to the erection of that building, because I was of opinion then, as I am now, that the duty of a government is to go ahead of the trade, not to allow itself to lag behind it. I knew that the trade of Halifax would not come immediately. But that elevator in Halifax is an invitation to the trade. My hon. friend's elevator in St. John, I believe, is not doing very much either. But I do not care for that-the accommodation is there, and I have always supported him faithfully on the ground I have stated, that I believe In the complete and speedy equipment of our national harbours. Speaking from that standpoint, I do not hesitate to say that the policy of the government to-day is a mistaken policy. Why ? We have spent, as I have said, $70,000,000 on our system of canals. We are going to spend millions upon millions to secure further railway accommodation. Where do we wish the trade to go ? Through the St. Lawrence route. Mr. Hays, speaking elsewhere a few days ago said what is perfectly true, that we
vsJ

mo providing accommodation in the west, but we do not do anything for ' the spout ' in the east. The port of Montreal, as it is equipped to-day cannot handle the trade that is coming to it. If my hon. friend would do us the pleasure of visiting our harbour now, he would find that there is not enough accommodation. A few days ago there were fifty large steamers in the port of Montreal. We are developing, deepening, widening the St. Lawrence river ; we are lighting it in a first-class manner ; we are going to spend even more money than we have spent in the past in completing all our other equipment. Yet, at the very most important strategic point we put up a wall against the trade. There is no sense in sueh policy. The government of which I was lately a member understood the position better in the past than it does to-day, because they agreed to a proposition of mine which is now being carried out, to complete, at federal expense, the harbour accommodation in the eastern portion of the port of Montreal. And what has been the result of that wise policy that my hon. friends followed with me in the past ? The Canadian Pacific Railway Company have located in the eastern part of Montreal their large works, works that will employ about eight thousand people. The Grand Trunk Railway Company, in view of the improvements going on in Montreal, have agreed to erect an elevator and warehouses. Is not this the best evidence that when we move in the path of progress we are rewarded immediately ?
I am very much surprised at the statement made by the Minister of Finance a few minutes ago. He said : You cannot expect to have freight sheds. What he calls sheds are a necessary equipment of the harbour, that you find in every port in the world. Go to any well equipped harbour, and you will find that a bare wharf is not an equipment; you must have warehouses, you must have trade, you must have all the modern appliances that have made such nations as Germany, France, England and the United States so successful in the trade of the world. To the south of us we have neighbours who have magnificently equipped harbours. Why should we not have the same ? Trade has been diverted from us, a great deal of our own trade is finding its way through American channels. When trade has once been diverted it is a difficult thing to get it back. The only thing we have to do is to give better rates, better accommodation, just as good rates and accommodation as other nations are giving. Unless we make up our minds to give as low rates as possible, to give as good equipment as money can make, we cannot expect to be rewarded to any large extent for the expenditure we are incurring now. Parliament was asked yesterday to guarantee for thirty years a loan for $9,000,000 for a railway in the west. That railway company will not send their trade to the St. Law-Hon. Mr. TARTE.
rence route unless you give them good rates. That railway company goes through Minnesota, Duluth is very near by, the United States routes are available; and I say again that unless you make the St. Lawrence route cheap, commodious and safe, you cannot expect trade.
Now, I think that on reflection the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches will admit that the views that I am stating-not now for the first time, I have stated them when I was their colleague, privately and on the floor of parliament-are correct views. When I was Minister of Public Works I tried to carry out those views, and with the help and co-operation of the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues I succeeded in beginning improvements and the equipment of our harbours in nearly all parts of the country. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) is not doing justice to the government when he says, when he seems to imply, that we have not done anything. It is not fair to speak in that way. Large things cannot be done in a day, but the beginning is there, and a good beginning it is. There has been great improvement in the port of Montreal. I obtained from this parliament the sanction of a vote of $1,000,000 for the port of Quebec. Three Rivers is being equipped. I went to the port of St. John last year, on an electoral occasion, when the Minister of Railways, speaking of my visit, said that I was a very pleasant little man, and had gone down to the sea to offer public works. I went down at the request of the citizens, of the board of trade, of the merchants, to look into the accommodation which is necessary. I have no hesitation in stating here that the government should equip at their own expense the port of St. John better than it has been equipped in the past. There is not enough accommodation there. They are doing it to some extent in granting, as we did some time ago, a three percent guarantee to a private company for a dry-dock. But that is not doing what I would like to see done. The government should equip these harbours themselves. The Minister of Public Works should take hold of these national harbours. When I was a minister I was often accused of monopolizing things. I cannot be accused of such a desire now. There is no fear that 1 shall be minister again very soon, so I am speaking independently when I say that this is a genuine national policy that should be followed by this government. Whoever may be Minister of Public Works, as a rule, he understands his business and his duty. I would trust these large national undertakings to any Minister of Public Works, whoever lie may be. Therefore, I earnestly beg the government to think twice over the position they are taking to-day. I quite understand that it is too late to recede from the position they have assumed in reference to the port of Montreal, although they are

going back on what they have said in the past. Because the fact that we had agreed to build at national expense part of the equipment that is now being carried out in tlie port of Montreal, was a sanction of the principle that in future the port of Montreal would be treated as Port Colborne is treated, as Parry Sound is treated, as Fort William is treated, as Quebec is treated. I do not complain of the treatment afforded to these towns, I am glad to see it; I only want to remind the House and the country of the fact that Montreal is the most important port. It is really the largest port, and therefore should require our earnest aid. With these few remarks, Mr. Chairman, and reserving the privilege of dealing with the question again, I resume my seat.

I listened carefully to gather from the speeches of my hon. friends from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) exactly what position they were taking witli regard to the resolution now before the committee. If I could come to any conclusion it was that they were not offering any particular opposition, but they were of the opinion that the port of Montreal was in some way being discriminated against, and was not being treated, if I heard their language correctly, as well as other ports throughout the country. I do not think the facts will bear that out. I believe this parliament has recently done a great deal towards developing the port of Montreal. The port of Montreal is not situated on the ocean, and in order to make It one of the great national ports of the Dominion it could not be treated in the same way as other places. Nor do I think the impression should be allowed to go abroad that the citizens of Montreal have done more towards the development of their harbour and shipping facilities than the citizens of any other port, large or small, throughout tile country. I think if my hon. friend will make comparisons he will find that in many of the smaller. ports on the lakes and on the ocean, the municipalities themselves have come forward and have contributed more to create the necessary facilities for shipping than the great city of Montreal lias done. I mention that only because the point seems to have been raised and the impression given that this port is being discriminated against, and not treated as well as other places. In regard to the statement of my hon. friend that the harbour commissioners will be bankrupt if they are called upon to pay interest upon the advances that have been made in the past and that which it is now proposed to make, I do not think there is any danger whatever. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has answered that when he said that it was not the opinion of the harbour commissioners, because they have applied for this loan and they have shown from the resources of the past
and from the resources which they will have In the future it will be quite easy for them to pay the interest upon the amount that has already been advanced and upon this $3,000,000, and retain something like $100,000 for the maintenance of the works under their charge. As to the treatment which has been accorded the harbour of Montreal in the past, I find, according to tlie books of the department, that over $13,000,000 has been expended on tlie port of Montreal. Out of that amount the parliament of Canada has contributed something over $8,000,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. .Tames Sutherland).

speechtext: Upon loan.

No, not upon loan. On the development of the ship channel and improvements to the harbour something over $8,000,000 have been spent. Does my hon. friend say that it is not necessary to make improvements to the ship channel ?

I say that it is not any more necessary to the development of the trade of the country than the building of the canals is. Why. do you not charge the canals also to the port of Montreal ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC W'ORKS. Trade might have gone to other ports. One would suppose to hear those who are speaking about Montreal that the citizens of Montreal were taxed to pay the charges and the interest upon this loan.
They pay a good deal of it.

I do not take that view at all. I do not think any of them pay these charges, excepting those citizens who contribute to the trade of the country. The importers and exporters pay the fees that go to make up the interest that is paid upon these loans. I consider, so far as this large expenditure is concerned, that it is correctly chargeable to the port of Montreal. It may be said that this is a national port, that its development is necessary in the interest of the country, but the same thing can be said, in a comparative degree, regarding the development of any other port or channel throughout the country which is in the interest of the general trade of the country. Now, I am pointing this out because it appeared to me that there was a desire to give a wrong impression to the House and the country as to the actual state of affairs in regard to the improvements which have been made and which are being made at the port of Montreal. I think, whatever may be the future policy of the country in regard to this port, we are not prepared to say that every port in the country, both great and small, shall De declared to be free. As has been pointed out by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, the question as to what action may be taken towards decreasing the fees collected upon mer-

ehandise received and delivered at these ports may be one for consideration, but so far as the general benefit derived by the parties using the elevators, warehouses, sheds and other works that are provided by public contribution is concerned, I think it is only right that those directly using them should contribute something for the advantage which they derive from their use. In the meantime, at any rate, that will be continued as the policy of the government. The port of Montreal, as my hon. friend says, may not be fully equipped for all the trade that will come to it, but the advances which have been made in the past and the liberal advance now being made, I think, if properly expended, will put the port of Montreal in better shape than it is to-day for doing business. We all hope the development of the trade of the country will be such at the port of Montreal, that greater facilities and greater improvements will be required, and I have no doubt that when the time comes this House will be ready to support any proper suggestion that may be brought down for the continuance of the improvements. The completion of the improvements now suggested and for which this money will make provision, I think, will do a great deal towards making the port of Montreal just what my hon. friend said it should be-a great national port. The general question of transportation comes into speeches made on an occasion of this kind. I am always listening attentively to hear what practical suggestions may be made. It is all very well to get up in this House, or on the platform, and talk about the importance of the transportation question, but what we want are practical suggestions as to what would be the best policy to adopt. So far as I am concerned, my greatest desire at the present time is to gain information of a practical character-, and that instead of discussing the question in an academic manner on the platform and in the House, we may have the advantage of listening to some practical, business-like suggestions that can be carried out to the advantage of the country.
Mr. ROBERT BICKERDIIvE (Montreal, St. Lawrence). Mr. Chairman, I may state that I agree very largely with what the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) have said on the auestion of making the port of Montreal a national port and a free port. But we are met at the present time with the fact that we have to continue the improvements that we started some years ago. There is no other way to do it than by borrowing this $3,000,000, and there is no way we can get it without paying interest for it. I would have been very pleased if the government had seen their way clear to giving that money without charging any interest, but that is not the policy of the government at present, nor do I think that it was the policy of the Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
preceding government. I must say that I think the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), in charging the cost of the St. Peter channel to Montreal, is hardly fair to us. I do not think it is any fairer that the Lake St. Peter channel should be chargeable to the city of Montreal than that the Welland canal should be chargeable to the city of Toronto. They are all canals. I have a very good authority on that question, the late lamented statesman that we all thought so much of, the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie. He said that the canals of this country should not be chargeable to any particular part of the country, but to the whole country, as the whole country is benefited by them. The hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's, says that the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) takes a narrow view of matters pertaining to the city of Montreal. I will not quarrel with him in that statement, but I am rather surprised that the hon. gentleman, when he was Minister of Public Works, did not soften the hon. Minister of Finance towards the city of Montreal. That would have been the time for the hon. gentleman to have used his influence. Not only was he Minister of Public Works, but, if report says correctly, he was also the master of the administration, and as such surely that was the time for the hon. gentleman to have insisted upon the government doing their duty towards Montreal. I believe they have not done so. I believe no government has done so. It is a fact that up to the present day not one dollar of public money has been spent upon the harbour of Montreal for which interest has not been paid. It is true that the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works did start, and that the government are now continuing, the building of a portion of the harbour of Montreal at the public expense. It is not really in the city of Montreal, as the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's, knows well. It is a good work that the government are carrying on, and we take no exception to it. It is not the intention of the harbour commissioners to raise the tolls. No man knows better than the hon. member for Jacques Cartier and the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's, that within the last two or three years the tolls have been reduced by from 20 to 25 per cent.

It would be impossible to raise them.
Mr. BICKERDIIvE. The hon. member for St. Mary's was consulted in the matter at that time. He thought the reduction was not enough and we cut down the tolls until there was a 40 per cent reduction. It would be impossible to reduce them further. The intention is to charge the steamship companies and they willingly agree to pay it if you give them first class double-decked steel sheds in which they can do their business at much less expense than they are doing it at now. We all know that the

harbour of Montreal is very much congested and that goods are lying all ov'er the wharfs. We will supply splendid storage facilities under this scheme and these men are willing to pay for that to the extent of the interest on the loan. Therefore if we spend $2,000,000 on sheds, these sheds will really pay for themselves. I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) in his statement that the port of Montreal is bankrupt at the present time. The port of Montreal ha,s always paid every dollar of the interest on the advances made to it, and, Sir, I believe that if there was any danger of the port of Montreal becoming bankrupt the citizens of Montreal are loyal enough to their port to not allow it to become bankrupt. I believe the day is coming when not only the port of Montreal but all the ports of the Dominion, and especially those on the St. Lawrence and the Atlantic coast, will be made free to commerce. We must have free ports in Canada if we are going to compete successfully with the United States. There is no question about that, and I believe that this government will come to that conclusion. I think theyi see it now, but they are probably not just ready to do it, as no doubt there are a great many things they would like to do but cannot do at the present moment. But, Sir, I hope that next year the government will take over the port of Montreal and assume the debt. I hope they will do the same thing with Three Rivers, Sorel and Quebec. The only way in which we can keep the ports of Canada on a par with the ports in the United States is by making them free ports, and making the commerce of the country as free from tolls as possible. As to the elevator, I expect that it will pay its way when it gets running. We will then have a debt of between $10,000,000 and $11,000,000, but I must frankly say that it will not be sufficient to finish the work there. On the most conservative estimate I can make, it will take $12,000,000 to put the port of Montreal in good shape. If the government cannot see their way clear now to make Montreal a free port they might reduce the interest and if the debt were $12,000,000 and the interest were 21 per cent there would be very little difficulty about raising the funds. Another thing the government might do is this :	They might at
least pay to the city of Montreal and the harbour commissioners the money they owe them. It is well known to the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that the government owes to the harbour at Montreal nearly $2,000,000, which was left over from the old Lake St. Peter debt, and which was charged up to the harbour commissioners. I trust that at an early date the government will pay this just debt which they owe to the port of Montreal.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) at the
beginning of his speech said that when I was in office I should have commenced by getting public money far the port of Mont-eral, but knowing the facts as he does, he was obliged to correct that statement and to add that there are works at Montreal which have been carried out at the public expense, although he said these works were not in the port of Montreal proper. Well, the port of Montreal is the one thing.
I said they were not in the city of Montreal.
The hon. gentleman used the very words I attributed to him.
I did not mean it.

I will take the hon. gentleman's correction. My hon. friend (Mr. Bickerdike) who is a harbour commissioner knows that to-day there is a very large trade which is being developed in the eastern portion of the harbour. When I was a minister I had the honour of bringing my colleagues to the principle that the port of Montreal as a national port should be equipped in future at the public expense. That work has been begun and my hon friend has expressed the hope that next year the government will give full recognition to that principle. I hope so. The hon. gentleman thought fit to allude to the fact that I was supposed to be the master of the administration. Well, the facts do not prove that.
Hear, hear.
It is of course quite true that every Prime Minister does not take the same severe view of his colleagues' speeches as the Prime Minister of Canada took of mine.
Hear, hear.

I have on my desk a very important speech delivered yesterday in the Imperial House of Commons in which Mr. Balfour says very distinctly that he had no desire to discipline his colleagues in the way some people expected he would discipline them. I was not the master of the administration^ but I tried to be the master of my own mind.
Hear, hear.

My mind was that we should endeavour to develop to the best of our ability the trade of this country on Canadian and national lines. I tried to bring about that result. However, if next year the government comes down with a policy which will better suit our views, I will be the first man to applaud and cheer them. My hon. friend from St. Lawrence knows very well that this $3,000,000 will not equip the port of Montreal, and that it will be necessary to spend a very much larger amount of money. There is no use hiding the facts. What is $10,000,000 to a great national harbour ?
Is it proposed that dues and fees shall be collected upon the works which are being constructed in that portion of the harbour which is not in the city of Montreal ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes. I stated to the House after having discussed the matter with my colleagues, that those works when completed would be treated just in the same way as other works.
That was the understanding.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes.
How much better off is the harbour then ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The harbour commissioners are not paying interest on that money, and it is the beginning of lowering the tolls.
But you are continuing to charge tolls ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: My hon. friend is not serious. If the public treasury gives $2,000,000, the harbour commissioners have not to pay the interest on it, and there is so much less to be charged on the port of Montreal. Surely the hon. minister has not thought twice. I will try to make myself clear.
You will have some difficulty in doing so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The difference is just this. That when money is not borrowed we have no interest to pay on it.
When the hon. gentleman says : * We have no interest to pay on it; ' who are the 'we' ?
The country.
The country pays it one way or the other.
I am speaking as a Canadian member of parliament having at heart the development of Canadian trade through Canadian channels. Why have we spent about $20,000,000 on the Intercolonial Railway ?
That is not the question.

It is the question. It is on the same lines, because we expect to have more trade. Why are our hon. friends asking us to guarantee millions upon millions for railway companies if not to have more trade ? The harbour of Montreal should be treated on the same lines as the railways, for the same reason. It seems to me that the position I am taking is the right one. We have this year made the canals free. In saying we, I speak as a member Hon. Mr. TARTE.
of parliament, for on that question parliament was unanimous.

May I ask my hon. friend a question ? I fail to understand him so far. Will he kindly point out what is the distinction from which the port of Montreal benefits, between paying dues and fees on works which are not under the control of the harbour commissioners, and paying the same measure of dues and fees on works which are under the control of the harbour commissioners ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It seems to me that the answer is very easy. The policy which I was endeavouring to impress on my colleagues, and which I thought I succeeded in impressing upon them, was that the port of Montreal should be made as free a port as it was possible to make it. Then, by our constructing, at the public expense, some of the works of improvement which are now going on, and the harbour commissioners having no money to borrow, they would have no interest to pay. The country would supply the money, and there would be so much less interest to pay.
Who would pay it ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is another small herring my hon. friend is drawing across the trail.
I think that is very much like a whale, instead of a small herring.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I may be slow, but I do not see the wit of the word. Seriously speaking, what I was aiming at when I had the honour of being a colleague of my hon. friend, was to impress on the government and the country the necessity of having as cheap transportation as it was possible to make it. That is the reason why I have always been happy to help my friends in the maritime provinces to get accommodation for that part of the country. It is the reason why I have been preaching this gospel of transportation from one end of the country to the other ; and I thought I had succeeded in impressing upon the government the necessity of not saddling the port of Montreal with any more debt. Suppose we take the position that the port of Montreal shall pay for past debts, but that for the future it should be equipped at the national expense. That is in two words what I was aiming at then, and what I am aiming at now. I quite admit that it would be difficult to make the port altogether free, because there will always be the cost of maintenance; but I do not know that the time will not come when public opinion will be so strong that even this government, which seems to be very steep at times on matters of national importance, will be obliged to realize that the sentiment of the nation is above party ex-

pediency. I say without any hesitation that the policy followed to-day is one of party expediency, because my hon. friends may be afraid to be reproached elsewhere for giving money to the port of Montreal. Well, we must recognize that geography cannot be changed. The port of Montreal has been placed where it is by the hand of Providence. It is the first port at the end of the lakes, at the head of navigation. I heard one of my colleagues say the trade could go elsewhere. Where could it go ? It could not stop farther up without going to American ports, such as Portland, New York, Philadelphia, and other ports. Quebec will undoubtedly have its trade, but Quebec has always been where it is. To-day the port of Montreal is there, with its magnificent natural facilities ; and, m spite of the fact that we have no great accommodation at Montreal, the trade is coming to that port, because trade is always inclined to go as far as possible into the land-this my hon. friends know as well as I do, if not better. It seems to me, then, that the policy that this country should follow is to make the port of Montreal and other ports of national importance as free as it is possible to make them. St. John, Halifax, Quebec, Three Rivers, should be made commodious and cheap ports, such as Canadian energy and Canadian enterprise and Canadian money can make them. This is not a sectional question with me. I recognize all the ports that are of national importance as forming part of the same system, and, unless we so recognize them, we shall be left behind. By improving the waterways you give competition and cheap rates to the farmers and the industrial interests, and you serve a great national object.

Mr. Chairman, no one can deny that my hon. friend invariably makes every subject he discusses in this House interesting, if not in itself, at least to those who listen to him. He has just now spoken of Montreal as having been placed where it is by the hand of Providence. I do not think there can be any doubt that Montreal is at the point where the rapids in the St. Lawrence begin and where the river navigation, properly so-called ends, as the act of Providence ; but I think Providence had very little to do with the digging of the channel between Quebec and Montreal. I think we have to give some credit to man for the part he has taken in connection with the works of construction that have been carried on in order to enable Montreal to occupy the position it now occupies. My hon. friend talks of making Montreal a national port. There is some vagueness and uncertainty as to what he means by a national port. Ho I understand that he means a port equipped with wharfs, sheds, and elevators at the national expense, to be used by ail-comers for nothing? If that is what he means by a national
port, in order to put Montreal on an equal footing with the other harbours of this Dominion, shall we not do the same thing for the other harbours ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: Hear, hear.

Why distinguish ? If we do that, it means that we must expend upon them a certain amount of money which comes out of the public exchequer, and on that money somebody must pay the interest. The people of Canada at large must pay the interest on that. Where is the difference in principle between paying the interest on money that would be expended in that way, and getting the interest back as we now do, out of the pockets of those who use the goods that go to the port of Montreal and get the benefit of these improvements ? Is that uot the more intelligent way, if I might use the word, of disposing of this matter-that those who use these improvements created by Canada shall pay for the use they make of them ? My hon. friend says that we ought to equip our ports in a way to fit them to compete with the American ports. I can speak of New York . there is not an inch of wharf in the city of New York that is not paid for by the city.
There is not an inch of wharf nor a foot of shed in New York which is not paid for. All those improvements made in the harbour of New York are paid for by those who use them. Why should we depart from the principle here ? Why should a different policy be followed in our Canadian ports ? It seems to be almost unavoidable that m.v hon. friend and myself should occasionally indulge in a little controversy with reference to the port of Quebec. I have no desire to enter into any discussion for the purpose of making parochial politics, and I am quite willing to admit that both my hon. friend and I are animated by the same spirit and desire to do all we can to advance the interests of our Canadian ports. My hon. friend knows that about three million dollars were spent on the port of Quebec. He knows too how that money was spent and to what extent we benefited by it. The result of the expenditure, as my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) told us the other night, is that we have in the Louise basin a berth for one ship. My hon. friend from St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) talks of the expenditure in Quebec made by the government and for which no return was made to this government, but what occurred ? No sooner was the expenditure begun than immediately, for the purpose of drawing away the trade which the expenditure was intended to benefit, seven million dollars were expended on the channel between Quebec and Montreal. I am not questioning the right of the people of Montreal to use all their energies for the purpose of getting this expenditure of public money on the improvement of the waterway, but

I am simply pointing out that, as a matter of fact, it absolutely neutralized the expenditure on the part of Quebec. The expenditure was made absolutely useless because, in the first place, the money was expended at an improper place, and then, in the second instance, the government of the day immediately proceeded to expend millions on the lake St. Peter channel, in order to divert the shipping from Quebec to Montreal. I am not finding any fault with the government of that day for improving the channel, for we are going on the same lines, but I am simply pointing out how the port of Quebec was affected by that policy. My hon. friend must not forget that not only did we spend $7,000,000 In deepening that channel but that we are also spending at the rate of some $600,000 per annum on the maintenance of the channel, we are expending in the vicinity of from $800,000 to $900,000 on capital account for the construction of two dredges to be used in improving that channel. When we come to build elevators, there is no reason why we should make any distinction between Montreal and Quebec. We have two elevators in Quebec, built by private corporations. If the Montreal Harbour Board thinks it proper to build one in that port, I have no desire to interfere, but, the least the general public can ask is that those who use the elevator should be made to pay for it. We are asked to build sheds in addition to the elevators. Is there any good reason why those who use the sheds should not pay for that use ? We have built sheds in Quebec but without any government aid. I do not wish to detain the House, but it seems to me that if we adopt the principle of equipping Montreal as a national port at the public expense, in all fairness we should do the same for all the other ports in the Dominion. Quebec has greater natural advantages than Montreal, and if Montreal had not been so generously aided by the hand of man, the trade which is done there would be centred in Quebec. I go further and say, that until the government interfered for the purpose of building this channel between Quebec and Montreal, and so long as Quebec was left with its natural advantages, it was in advance of Montreal. I can remember when we had ten ships in that port for one in Montreal ; and although things have been changed since, that change is due to the result of government expenditure. In saying this, I am not casting any reflection on that policy. I am quite free to admit that whatever is to the advantage of Montreal, profits every other part of Canada. But, I would urge that all the ports in the Dominion be put on the same footing and each be given a fair field and no favour.

My hon. friend and myself will agree no doubt as to facts of public notoriety. The port of Quebec was equipped in the same convenient way as Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
the port of Montreal is being equipped now, namely, by a loan. If there is any one who knows how that money was spent, I am the one. My hon. friend knows a good deal, but perhaps I know more than he does, I know a good deal about it, but let by-gones be by-gones. We ventilated that question some years ago, and I hope that we will see nothing more of the kind in the future. There are some facts which my hon. friend seems to have forgotten. He says that in Quebec we are building sheds and not asking anybody for money to build them ? Well, I give my hon. friend the credit for the interest he has displayed in the port of Quebec by inducing the government to forfeit the rights guaranteed to it by the bonds in the hands of the hon. Finance Minister. The government gave up the precedence attaching to those bonds in order to enable the people of Quebec to borrow money.

Eet my hon. friend state the facts fully. In so far as that precedence is concerned, it had reference to the piece of wharf built immediately opposite the custom house. The money was spent on the construction of that wharf and had absolutely no connection with the sheds.

The sheds were built because the government gave up its precedence, and I am very glad it did so. The harbour commissioners at Quebec owe about $6,000,000 with the interest. I fully recognize that they cannot pay either the capital or the interest. I fully admit that a large volume of that money has been badly spent, but all the same the government advanced the money and has never been paid the interest. I am not complaining of this, but I say that the port of Montreal has not been treated in a like manner. That port pays the interest on every dollar borrowed from the government. It is not the people of Montreal who pay, but the trade of the country ; and if the trade of the country is obliged to pay rates that are too high, it will go through other channels. That cannot be denied. The port of Quebec has natural advantages. My hon. friend has said that the dredging of the St. Lawrence has diverted the trade from Quebec, but he forgets that the work of dredging the St. Lawrence began nearly fifty years ago- long before the Louise Basin was started.
But the diversion did not take place until about fifteen years ago. Before that we had more ships in Quebec than in Montreal.

I shall not discuss that point The trade is taking good care of itself. My hon. friend knows that most of the important harbours of the world are inland harbours. He knows that Hamburg and Manchester are both inland harbours.

Why the German nation have spent $75,000,000 on the Elbe and Hamburg works.
They have no ocean harbours.

Well, there is no use discussing such a question before such an audience. The port of Quebec is available; why, then, does the trade seek the port of Montreal ? Because the port of Montreal is the natural centre of exchange between the west and the east. Why should a barge loaded with grain pass by Montreal, when there are sea-going ships waiting for her cargo? The city of Montreal with its suburbs and surroundings has a population of nearly half a million. Why should they displace themselves and send their trade elsewhere ? That cannot possibly be done. Why did we build the canals ? To take the trade through the St. Lawrence route. It seems to me that it is not necessary to adduce much argument to establish the position I take. My hon. friend has spoken of the port of New York. That port is fairly well equipped; but, on account of the high charges exacted there, it is losing ground every day.
How is it in Boston ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: How is it equipped ?
How are the charges ?
I have not the figures under my hand
How is it about the ownership of the wharfs, and the ownership of the sheds ?

In the United States, there are several systems. In certain cities, the state governments contribute, and in others the federal government contributes. Take Buffalo, for instance, that port has been equipped partly by the state government of New York, and party by the federal government. But we have to face the simple question :	Are we making up our
minds that we will give the trade cheap rates ? If so, we must take the means to do it. And the main reason why I object to the policy of my hon. friends on the treasury benches is that they are not taking the means to accomplish this great national object. However, we have made our position pretty clear. I hope that in the future my hon. friends will change their minds. If they do not change their minds we will try to induce the people outside to impress upon them the great importance of doing so.
My hon. friend from Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) said that $1,000,000 was voted last year for the harbour of Quebec. I have looked over the estimates and I find that only $100,000 was voted.

My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) is a very clever man. But he is doing now just what the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) tried to do-he is drawing a red herring across the trail. And let me explain to the committee how he is doing it. When I had the honour of being Minister of Public Works, I was approached, and the right hon. the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was approached at the same time by the representatives of the trade of Quebec. They represented that it was necessary that there should be further equipment for the port. My right hon. friend helped me, and it was understood and agreed that certain works should be carried out. I placed the plans of those works on the Table of the House last session, works the carrying out of which would have involved the expenditure of about $1,000,000. My hon. friend has only to read ' Hansard ' to see that that is the case. I placed these plans on the Table with the consent of my colleagues, especially of the right hon. gentleman who leads the government. These plans were approved by the House. I asked for a vote of $100,000, of course, because we could not spend more during the present year; but at the time, I stated distinctly that these works would cost $1,000,000. These are the facts of the case. Now, my hon. friends have thought fit to change the plan. That is there business. What they are doing to-day is a good work-I do not complain that it is not a good work. But what I make bold to say to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is this-that if the government are going to provide this country with a fast Atlantic service, the accommodation being provided in Quebec is not sufficient. And if my hon. friend comes next year with an appropriation of the balance of the million dollars that I succeeded in getting, I shall be very glad to vote for it.

As my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has referred to me perhaps it will not be out of place for me to give a word of explanation as to the statement he has just made. My hon. friend laid before the House last year plans as to which there was a good deal of exception taken, and as to which, on the other hand, there was a good deal of approbation. These plans provided for the extension of the wharf at La Pointe J Carey, towards the middle of tlie river and works towards the back. I agreed that he should take an appropriation of $100,000 for the extension of the wharfs extending up to the wharf at La Pointe it Carey. As to the plans provided with regard to the extending of the works behind the Louise Basin, since I came back from Europe, it has been represented that there might be some danger to the existing works in carrying out the operations proposed. I asked my hon. friend the Minister of Public
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext:
Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) to have that matter decided before the work was gone on with. 1 agree with my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that the harbour has to be equipped; and, if we are to have, as we must have, a fast Atlantic service, considerable improvements must be added to give the accommodation necessary for that service. But whether we should go on with the plans that my hon. friend has provided for the extension of the work behind the Louise Basin is now under consideration. The plans are being considered by proper engineers, to see whether the plans proposed are correct or whether they should be amended.
As I am on my feet I may say a few words on the general topic under discussion. I take issue with my hon. friend in the view he has taken that the harbour of Montreal is being discriminated against. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) started that view. I took note of the statement he made, which, I think he himself will agree, requires some explanation. He said that we were dealing in a different way with the harbour of Montreal from the way in which we were dealing with the North-west. He said that we voted several millions yesterday for the North-west. That is true; but what we did for the North-west yesterday is precisely wrhat we propose now to do for the harbour of Montreal-in one case, as in the other we are simply loaning the credit of the Dominion. Yesterday it was to a big railway company to build a railway, and to-day it is to the Montreal Harbour Trust to carry on their work. I think there is no necessity of pushing the comparison further-we have only to state the case to show that there is no essential difference. But there is a matter of difference which I wish to point out. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has started the idea that the harbour of Montreal should be treated like every other harbour in the Dominion, that no more charges should be put upon it than upon any other harbour I agree with him. But my hon. friend should remember that we are to-day proceeding, with regard to the harbour of Montreal in a manner which, he will permit me to say, received his approbation when I had the honour of having him for my colleague. There is no difference between what is being done to-day and what was done three or four years ago. At that time we gave authority to the harbour commissioners of Montreal to borrow a certain amount to equip the harbour. At the same time we gave authority to my hon. friend, then Minister of Public Works, to carry out certain works in the harbour. He says that it was intended that these works should be made national works. So it was. I will not enter upon the discussion at this moment whether or not the works done by the government were to pay dues or not. That is not of material concern, -for X cannot see Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
that there is any difference, if dues are to be paid upon the wharfs, whether those wharfs are built by the government or by the harbour commissioners. In either case the tolls are to come out of the shipping, which seems to be a very sound principle. But at the same time that my hon. friend was obtaining authority from parliament to build these wharfs which are now in course of construction, which certainly are of great utility and will be of still greater utility in the future, the harbour commissioners were empowered to borrow money on the credit of the country to carry on their own works. I understand my hon. friend to say now that the harbour commissioners instead of spending the money themselves upon sheds and elevators, should not be allowed to do so, but that the money should be paid by the Minister of Public Works. That is practically his criticism. I have only to observe that there is no necessity and no opportunity at this moment, to change the policy which he inaugurated a few years ago.
My hon. friend remembers very well that when these works in the harbour of Montreal were contemplated he was Minister of Public Works. He gave a great deal of time to the plans which were prepared, and he knows very well that the equipment of these wharfs which it was then intended to build by the harbour commissioners was to be supplemented by elevators and by sheds. Therefore the hon. gentleman ought not to forget that at this moment we are simply carrying out the plans which had his sanction, and which were provided for three or four years ago to keep this harbour in the best possible condition for trade. It was not sufficient simply to have wharfs, it was not sufficient simply to have the necessary appliances for ships to load and unload their cargoes, but further works had to be done to provide an elevator and sheds for warehouses. Now is it not better, under such circumstances, that the authority which had begun these works should carry them to completion ? If in future we have other works to complete in the harbour of Montreal, as we shall have, then the views presented by my hon. friend may be presented with better purpose, and we shall have to decide then whether they should be built by the harbour commissioners or by the Minister of Public Works. All that will come in due time. In the meantime, I take notice of the objection made by my hon. friend that the harbour of Montreal ought not to be burdened more than any other harbour. Sir, if the harbour of Montreal has been more burdened than any other harbour-I do not say that it is so-whose fault is it ? It is certainly not the fault of this government. My hon. friend was for a sufficiently long time a member of this government to defend himself and to defend the government of which he was a member at the time. We found the situation when

we came in, we found the harbour commission of Montreal in possession of certain works. They applied to us to continue what they had been doing, and I give credit to my bon. friend for this, that he contributed a great deal, I think, to improve the work done by the harbour commissioners and to continue it. But if the harbour commissioners have spent too much money, if the harbour of Montreal has been unduly burdened, I think it is a case that the board of trade and the citizens of Montreal may be trusted to come and represent to the government. I received a notice a few days ago from the harbour board that they wanted to interview the government on this question and I granted the interview at once. Then they sent me word that they would come at a later period. When they come we will hear their views, and they will say whether the harbour of Montreal has been saddled with a greater burden than Toronto or St. John. But at this moment the hon. gentleman ought to agree that he can find no fault with us for doing what we are doing now, that is to say, for continuing the policy which he approved himself when Minister of Public Works, of enabling the harbour commissioners to carry on and complete the work which they had undertaken under his own regime.

The hon. gentleman, 1 am sure, will do me the justice to admit that when I had the privilege of being his colleague 1 always struggled, especially during the last couple of years, to have our national harbours equipped as fully as possible. He has in his hand a memorandum that I left two or three months before quitting office, in which my views are set forth very fully. I acknowledge that I have been a party to lending money to the port of Montreal, as I have also been a party to maintaining the tariff which is to-day in existence. There is always room for improvement in the world. It does not follow that because the port of Montreal lias been treated in the past in the way we know, we must always proceed in the same direction. I was glad to hear my hon. friend say that perhaps in the near future the direction in which we are proceeding now might be changed. I paid a good deal of attention to his words, and if I understood them correctly, it is good news for us, because the policy which is being followed now is not the right policy. We are at present only putting up a gate that we should instead be lowering. Only one word as to the work in Quebec. My right hon. friend has said that representations have been made to him that the plans I submitted to the House last year might perhaps imperil the existing works. I am sure that no engineer made such representations to him, because no engineer who knows anything about the works could say anything of the kind. I will explain to my right hon. friend. He
is not an engineer in public works, though he is a good engineer in some other directions. The works which were begun had no foundation ; we cannot dredge in the Louise Basin because the works have been laid without a foundation. The plan I submitted provided for a deeper foundation, about fifteen feet deeper, and at the same time to make it more solid. That makes a vast difference. My hon. friend I am sure did not mean to misrepresent me on that occasion.
I did not say it was a fact, I said that representations had been made.

There are representations that may be made with some motive. I know the cost of the Quebec harbour works. 1 have studied them carefully, but not in the direction that has been pointed out by my right hon. friend. There were some other interests, however, that I do not mean to allude to now.

The harbour commissioners of Montreal have treated this question in a businesslike way, and the government, I think, is treating the question in the same manner. There is no difficulty about the harbour commissioners being in a position to meet the interest on the loan which they have asked the Dominion government to make to them.
