The resolution which I hold in my hand, dated May 5tli, 1903, explains the position very well, there can be no misunderstanding about it:
Resolved, that should the loan of $3,000,000 asked for from the government be obtained, that about $2,000,000 would he required for building two storey steel sheds on the Alexandra, King Edward and Jacques Cartier piers, and the shore wharfs at sections 12, 13 and 17, which it is proposed to rent to the steamship lines, the rental to be charged therefor not to exceed six cents per square foot of space which, for 1,284,390 square feet which would be provided in the sheds, would yield $74,903.40 per annum, of which $60,000 would be for the interest, and the balance of $14,903.40 for maintenance and insurance. The interest on the balance of the loan of $1,000,000, which is $30,000, would be provided for out of the ordinary revenue obtained from wharfage" dues, as it is proposed to expend out of the aforesaid sum $586,885 on permanent paving, thus reducing the cost of annual repairs which in the past has been considerable for maintenance of roadways, and leave the expense which would be required for maintenance to be available for the payment of interest.
Now what are the facts ? The interest on the sums which we have authorized them to borrow, in all $10,222,000, will make, with the maintenance, a sum to he levied every year of $450,880. Now, if you deduct from that sum of $450,880, $30,000 of revenue from the elevator and $00,000, the rental on the sheds, you will have remaining a balance of $300,880 to provide for. The revenue last year was over $322,000,

so that there should be no fear whatever that the harbour commissioners will have sufficient to meet the Interest on the different sums that they have borrowed and those that they will borrow. Of course, it must be borne in mind that it will be only within the next few years that the whole amount can be borrowed because we can easily understand that the whole expenditure of this $3,000,000 cannot be made in one season. It would take two seasons at least in which this expenditure can be made. As regards the principle of advancing money to the harbour commissioners, I may say, as it has been said and repeated here, this is the same principle which has been in force since 1890 under this government. It is the same principle which has been applied by former governments. Well, if you look at the facts, in wlmt position are you ? In 1896 the former government were able to reduce the harbour dues in Montreal by from 25 to 30 per cent. Under the present government the harbour commissioners have been able, although they have reduced their interest, and although they have spent every year large sums of money for maintenance which they will not be called upon to expend in future years, when the wharfs will all have been paid for-they have been able, as I am perfectly well aware, and as has been stated by the hon. member for Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike), to reduce the dues by 40 per cent and notwithstanding this their revenue has been increasing. Fault has been found with this procedure by the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). I can only repeat what has been stated already that this principle was concurred in in 1898 and 1899 when the harbour commissioners came before the government and asked for advances, so that, if this is the time to find fault with the principle and to say that it is wrong it must have been equally wrong in 1898 and 1899. I want to go further. I say the principle is not wrong at the present time. There may come a time when all the harbours and piers will be perfectly free, but a'll this does not come in a day. It takes years before this can be accomplished. Take, for instance, the abolition of the tolls on the canals. For years and years the navigation companies had been asking that the tolls on the canals the customs dues and the inspection fees should be abolished. It is only this year that they have succeeded in obtaining justice, but this is a beginning and I think the present government cannot be accused of not doing anything to aid transportation and navigation when it is easy to calculate that the amount of which the navigation companies have been relieved is nearly $400,000 annually. Now, thq hon. ex-Minister of Public Works says that the principle is wrong and he states that he began himself the expenditure of public money to improve the port of Montreal. I have to Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
differ from him on that point, because, what he says as to the expenditure of public money to improve the port of Montreal means simply this that instead of the interest on that amount advanced for the construction of the pier in Hochelaga bay being paid indirectly to the government by the harbour commissioners it will be collected directly by the government in harbour dues at this pier, because nobody will deny that it was perfectly well understood when the money was voted to build this pier and when the consent of the harbour commissioners was asked that this pier, which is being built by Messrs. Poupore & Malone, would not be free but that dues would be charged at the same rate and under the same conditions as they are collected on the rest of the piers in the harbour of Montreal. Everybody understands perfectly well that in the case of the pier being built now under the control of the hon. Minister of Public Works, dues will be collected by the government instead of being collected by the commissioners and paid over to the government as interest.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Who will pay the interest on that $1,000,000 which will be spent at Hochelaga ?

It will be paid out of the dues. The government will pay the interest, but they will collect the amount hi dues on the pier. Blanc Bonnet et bonnet blanc. It means exactly the same thing, except, of course, that the debt of the harbour commissioners of Montreal will be increased by $600,000 or thereabouts, or by whatever may be the cost of the pier. As regards the position of the shipping interests and the trade of Montreal they will be in exactly the same position whether vessels land their goods and merchandise on the pier built by the government or whether they land their goods and merchandise on the piers built under the system adopted by the harbour commissioners. Now, a good deal has been said about the expenditure on the port of Montreal and on the channel. The facts as regards the expenditure of money on the channel ar.e fresh in the mind of every member in this House. The money spent on the channel of the St. Lawrence river between Montreal and Quebec was levied by the harbour commissioners of Montreal on the trade of Canada generally and on the shipping interest doing business in the city of Montreal. Great credit is due to the men of enterprise who, in 1840 or 1850, organized the harbour commissioners of Montreal and took in hand the work of improving the channel of the St. Lawrence which was then eleven or twelve feet deep on the flats of Lake	St. Peter and who
made it what it was in 1887 or 1888, when the government took hold of it. it was only fair and reasonable that the gov-

eminent, having taken charge of that channel, should assume the debt which had been contracted, although I think the government did not do entire justice to the harbour commissioners and citizens of Montreal, because, instead of reimbursing the whole amount that had been expended on the works of the channel they reimbursed only the capital expenditure without taking into consideration the interest. I know something about the matter, having been a member of the harbour commission for four years, and there is an account standing now awaiting settlement for interest paid on the sums advanced by the commissioners of nearly $2,000,000. Instead of pressing for the settlement of that claim against the government, the commission which is composed of men of business representing the vast corporations of Montreal, such as the Board of Trade, the Corn Exchange, the Shipping Interests, the Ghambre de Commerce, besides six members appointed by the government representing the best business men of Montreal, after having studied this question since 1898 have come to the unanimous opinion that it is a businesslike course to proceed in the way proposed. The general plans for the the improvement of the harbour of Montreal had been approved in 1898 by the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). These plans did not provide then for such works as permanent sheds, a complete railway track system, a steam crane and others which are included in the $3,000,000 loan. It is a well known fact that the harbour commissioners of Montreal are now in a better condition to execute these works properly and cheaply than any other body, because they have the whole organization at their disposal. They are in a position to undertake themselves works of this kind, except probably the steel structure which they will have to let by contract. The other works will be done u'nder the supervision of their own engineer and staff which up to the present time has proven itself to be perfectly competent. There is no fear of the Montreal harbour commissioners becoming bankrupt, or that the trade will be charged more for tolls than in the past. On the contrary, if you fake the trade this year since the opening of navigation which is only a comparatively short period, you will find that there were more head of cattle shipped up to the present time than during the whole season last year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

They have twelve steamers more in the port of Montreal this season than up to the corresponding date last season. I am informed by those who take a deep interest in our commerce that there have been shipped through the port of Montreal up to the present, 2,000,000 bushels
more of grain than during the corresponding period last year. That is probably due in part to the fact that tolls have been abolished on the canals, and that customs dues and inspection fees are no longer charged. As representing the largest division of the city of Montreal, I am entirely in accord with the proposition made by the harbour commissioners. It is the only reasonable proposition under the circumstances, and it is the best means calculated to equip the harbour of Montreal within a reasonable time. If the government were to take hold of these extensive works they would not have the necessary means and plant at their disposal, and It would take them a long time to get prepared for the work, while it Is the hope of every good citizen of Montreal that these works will be finished next season, and then the works can be proceeded with in the east end of Montreal which have been already started.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

I wish to add a word of correction and explanation. Touching the discrimination against Montreal, I am afraid my hon, friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) failed to catch the point of the question which I ventured to put him about the word ' we.' My only object was to emphasize the point Which has been made during the debate as to who pays the interest on the loan. My hon. friend said: ' We pay the interest,' which was likely to convey the impression that the people of Montreal pay the interest.
I did not mean that.

My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) admitted afterwards that this interest was paid by the trade of the country which passes through Montreal. As a matter of fact the citizens of the city of Winnipeg pay the Interest as much as the citizens of Montreal. There are cities in Canada where the people are paying hard money in taxes for harbour facilities, but Montreal is not one of them. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) and I differed as to the extent of the trade of Montreal. He said that in Montreal the total trade was nearly one-half the total trade of the country and I said I thought it was not more than 35 per cent. I see by the figures that last year it was actually 29-25 per cent. I do not mention that for the purpose of undervaluing it, because that is a very great proportion of the trade of the country. As the figures we use in debate are often quoted elsewhere it is just as well that the correction should be made.

I did not mean to say that the interest is paid by Montreal or elsewhere, but what I did try to urge was that unless you make the ports of Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax, cheap ports, the trade will not come to us at all. It is only from that standpoint that I am discussing the question.

I have been following this discussion with a good deal of interest, because I represent a constituency in which is situated one of the two principal Canadian seaports which are open all the year round. My constituents take a very deep personal interest in the question which is now to some extent uik^' discussion. I have been desirous of hearing from my hon. friends who are criticising the present proposal, some very cogent reasons why this vote ought not to be passed, because I felt convinced that if they made out a case strong enough to show that a great deal of argument was capable of being advanced against the approval of this motion, then a very j very strong case would be made in favour of the general adoption of the principle which the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) declares himself so strongly in favour of. There is no doubt that there is a difference between the manner in which some of the Canadian seaports are treated by this government and by all governments, and the manner in which other Canadian ports are treated. The Minister of Finance has correctly pointed out that the citizens of Montreal have not been called upon to pay any interest burden in connection with the expenditure upon their port.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The city of Montreal is contributing $1,000,000.
Now ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Now.

I was not aware of that fact, and the hon. gentleman permitted the statement of the Minister of Finance to pass unchallenged. If they have that in contemplation now, it is nevertheless the fact that up to the present moment the citv of Montreal has not put its hand into its poekets municipally speaking, and borne any por-Hon. Mr. TARTE.
tion of any charge incident to the betterment of their harbour. That cannot be said, as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has remarked, with regard to some other ports. It certainly cannot be said with regard to the seaport of St. John. When the business coming from the western country was being carried to St. John for ocean transport, which was bound to flow into that city, the people of St. John hoped that the government of the day would come to their assistance and enable them to handle that produce with advantage to the shippers and to the country. They could, I am free to confess, have secured assistance if they had been willing to place their harbour under the control of a trust, like one or two other harbours in the country. They did not agree to that, and therefore they received no direct assistance from the exchequer of Canada failing to get any assistance from the government of Canada, they set to work to provide the piers, sheds and other facilities, which were necessarily required if any business was to be done, by municipal taxation ; and a sum which exceeds three-quarters of a million and very nearly approaches a million dollars was actually paid by the people of that city in order to provide its harbour with these necessary requirements. The people of St. John are paying the tax on that expenditure. The business of the port does not bear it. There are no dues or fees collected in respect of the wharfs, because they had to be handed over to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in order that that company would interest itself in making St. j John a port of ocean shipment. The city has undoubtedly had some advantage from that expenditure. The business has increased arid is increasing year by year. I cannot at this moment state exactly the gross amount of tonnage shipped last winter as compared with previous years ; but it has quadrupled since these works were established. So that the committee can see that there was every warrant for the people of St. John, from the point of view of the interests of business, to embark ip this expenditure and provide the port with what it needed. But it appeared to me at that time, and it appears to me now, that we ought to appeal confidently for the support of the government; because if it is a fact that all these transportation and shipping facilities that have been provided by the government are of national importance and are justified from the national point of view, the nationdl interest does not cease to be involved when the shipment goes during the winter season from one of the Atlantic seaports. It is a national interest there if it is a national interest anywhere. My hope with regard to this-and it bears on the suggestion which the hon. member has made, that the government ought to make these ports free ports, and is a complete answer to any criticism that may be passed

upon us for making this vote-is that at the present moment the government, with the full knowledge of parliament, lias constituted a commission, the object of -which is to study the whole question as it bears upon the providing of proper facilities at the different Canadian seaports. Their business will be to look into the situation as respects them all, and to advise the government as to what, in their opinion, would be the proper method to pursue in order that those ports should be equipped in the manner which the national interests will require, and enable the business of the country to be transacted under the most favourable conditions. I cannot conceive of anything that ought to engage the more careful attention or consideration of this commission. I say, therefore, that it would be entirely premature, in view of the arrangements which have been made hitherto for the harbour of Montreal, to make any change at this moment in the matter under discussion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if it would not be wise to hold over even this vote until that commission has made its report ?

No ; if you did that, you would practically delay the improvements in the harbour of Montreal. These works, which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says were planned over ten years ago, have been partially performed. They -were taken hold of four or five years ago by the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works, and pushed on by the harbour trust with a considerable amount of energy. The plans contemplated the providing of sheds and other equipment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The plans of the sheds are ready now.

The plans of the sheds, I am told, are ready now, and it is a very serious matter to delay works of this kind. The harbour of Montreal has undoubtedly been suffering in the fact that it has not been able to furnish the required accommodation to the ships which came there last year. I have heard a number of shipping men say that they would have been willing to have their traffic carried through the port of Montreal if they had been confident that when it reached there, it would have got early shipping accommodation. I am very glad that the Harbour Trust of Montreal are prepared to go on with the work and push it rapidly to completion. One more word. My hon. friend, I think, ought to acknowledge that his criticism on this proposal of the government is not timely or justifiable. My hon. friend's language was that the government ought not to have refused to give money, and ought not to have insisted on the Harbour Trust of Montreal 141
taking this money by -way of a loan, as these resolutions provide. I do not think my hon. friend, as an "ex-minister, and as one having so much to do with this question as a minister, was justified under all the circumstances, in getting up in his place and, without proper reflection and consideration, condemning the government for carrying out the very arrangements he warmly advocated when he was a member of the government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Am I not advocating now what I did in the government for two or three years ?
We must not tell.
Outside of it, then ?

I do not find fault with the hon. gentleman for advocating what he advocates ; but advocacy is one thing, and criticism and condemnation of his late colleagues is another thing, for doing what he favoured and justified and arranged, and what they must do if his arrangements are to be carried out. What I complain of is that he says that the government should not have refused to give the harbour commissioners this money, and should not force them to take it as a loan. I say that criticism is unfounded, and I am surprised that my hon. friend should be so unmindful of the views and opinions he has held heretofore as to make that criticism on the present proposal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I would like just to offer an observation or two, and 1 must begin by saying to my hOn. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) that he surprised me a little in proposing, in an off-hand way, that the prosecution of these important works and the voting of this money should be postponed. My hon. friend, like many of his colleagues from the west, is always ready to urge the needs of the -west in connection with this very question of transportation ; but I have often noticed that once they get to this end of Lake Superior, my hon. friend and some of his colleagues do not realize the importance of this end of the question. I cannot understand -what my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) means when he says that, with respect to the wharf which we built below Montreal, we are in the same position as we are with respect to these projected works. The country in that case gave the money and there is no interest to pay. but in this case the government loans the money and there is interest to pay, so that I fail to understand how both cases are the same. Of course, as the hon. gentleman says, we collect harbour dues, but not as interest on the money.
I regret that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance should have seen in what I said



a desire to defend parochially the rights of Montreal. It was not in any local spirit that I approached this question. I view it as the general question of transportation. I have no interest in the harbour myself. My constituency lies outside the city, and I brought this matter before the House because I consider that in some parts of the country we are dealing with the transportation system in a different manner than we are dealing with it in other parts. In 1901 we collected $270,000; and if we are to accept the statement of the lion. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, last year we collected a little more. But we cannot, without sacrificing, not only the port of Montreal but any other port that we may wish to nationalize, collect such a sum as $400,000, and that would be the least we would have to collect. The hon. Minister of Finance talks of the warehouses that are going to be built out of the $2,000,000. He is mistaken. It is sheds that we are building.
A rose by another name will smell as sweet.

There is a greater difference than my hon. friend will admit. When he talks of a warehouse he is talking of something that will produce large revenue, but we cannot have very much revenue out of those sheds. The charges now are too heavy and should be reduced, but we will never be able to reduce them under this system. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has fallen into the old system of complaining about Montreal taking away the trade of Quebec. That is absurd. The deepening of the St. Lawrence was not made with the object of ruining Quebec but of meeting the demands of trade. We have no grudge against Quebec. We are glad that considerable business is being done there, but we cannot shut our eyes to the fact that vessels all the world over will go as far inland as possible. My hon. friend must not forget that at present the port of New York is in a state of more or less decadence on account of its charges, and ships are going elsewhere. They go to Baltimore, Boston, Portland and other ports.
There are harbour dues at all these ports.
There are and must be everywhere, but we must reduce them. If we want to compete with the American ports successfully, we must reduce our charges.
There are no harbour-dues in New York.

It comes to the same thing. There are charges and very heavy charges to be paid in New York. They take the shape of rentals, but it does not make much difference. I do not know what my right hon. friend meant when he said that" it was Montreal's oiwn fault if it is liable for this Mr. MONK.
large amount on which we cannot pay interest. It is not our fault, but is due to the situation of the harbour. These plans, which were made long ago, must be carried out, and for that the citizens of Montreal are not to blame.
The majority of the harbour commissioners are government appointees.

The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. PrSfontaine) was not exactly of the same opinion some months ago. He believed then that the harbour commissioners should be thrust aside and that the improvements to the harbour were so important that they should be carried out by himself. That point, however, I shall not discuss now. I would like to say to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals that we have given money in Montreal for the improvement of the harbour and have made great improvements in the approaches to the harbour and spent considerable sums of money. I might inform him also that in St. John the harbour charges collected go into the civic revenue. If that be the case, it makes a considerable difference. So that on the whole, I was right in saying that the government are to blame.
The ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) told us a few moments ago that this nationalization of our ports-he did not speak of Montreal alone-was approved of by this government at the time he was one of the ministers, and I really so understood by words which fell from several of the ministers at the time. What I find fault with is that these hon. gentlemen are to-day going back on that policy. Unless we adopt that system for the port of Montreal and the other important ports of the Dominion, then the millions we have spent and the millions we pledged to spend on railways will be to a large extent useless.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Public Works has asked for practical suggestions, and I shall venture to offer him one. The hon. Minister of Finance said that it was the intention of the harbour commissioners of Montreal to spend $1,000,000 on an elevator and $2,000,000 in building a shed or warehouse, and that the revenue from the elevator would pay the interest on the $1,000,000 and the revenue from the shed or warehouse would pay the interest on the $2,000,000. But who is going to pay that ? If we put a million dollars into an elevator, who are going to use it but the farmers ? Who will pay the tolls but the farmers and not the people generally. Who will pay the rent of the shed ? The steamship companies, in the first place, but from whom will they collect it ? From the agriculturists of this country.
The charges are raised on the goods themselves.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It Is the steamship company that raises them.
No, the harbour commissioners themselves.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And it comes straight out of the pockets of the farmers. If I buy a million bushels of wheat in the North-west, the water rate from Port Arthur to Montreal is four or five cents a bushel, and to Europe another four or five cents per bushel. But if this elevator, which my hon. friend is going to erect at the port of Montreal, is going to charge a quarter or a half of a cent for transhipping from the barges to the ocean going steamers, I will have to buy from the farmer at half a cent a bushel less than if the elevator were free. Let the government, in place of loaning these 83,000,000, hand the cash over as a gift to the harbour commissioners of Montreal, so that they may make these improvements without increasing the tolls. Let us have no tolls charged the farmers on this expenditure, for they are the parties who will* have to pay and not the general public. Let the government make this a national port, let them give this 83,000,000 out and out, and I am sure that the people of Ontario and the Dominion generally will be pleased to see Montreal made a national free port. We cannot compete successfully unless we have lower rates. If I have a million bushels of grain at Port Arthur to be shipped to Europe, and I get a ten cent rate by Boston and also a ten cent rate by the Canadian route together with these elevator charges, the grain will have to be shipped by Boston. One sixteenth of a cent will transfer the traffic from the Canadian to the American route, and this elevator charge at Montreal may have the effect of sending all the grain by the United States, and so we shall get no revenue whatever. There should be no elevator charges upon grain shipped from Port Arthur by the St. Lawrence route to a foreign market. Any charge that is maclc comes out of the pockets of the farmers of the North-west, or Ontario, or wherever the grain is grown. It comes out of the pockets [DOT]of the farmers, and not out of the pockets of the people generally.

I spoke of the people of Canada generally, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) is giving a meaning to the words that I did not intend. What I meant was that the charges had to be paid by those concerned in the traffic. I am as much a friend of the farmer as anybody. But I believe that if the farmer put his grain in a warehouse, he should pay for the privilege ; if he puts it in his own barn he pays for the barn. I believe the farmer is ready to pay for any service that is rendered to him. Of course, we might easily give free warehouse accommodation, or-yes, as an hon. friend belli*
sides me suggests, we might pay the freight from Winnipeg ; we might throw in cliro-mo ; we might offer many advantages ; but these are not business. We believe the farmer should be treated like a man. As touching the question of these trifling sheds, -to cost about 82,000,000-to which the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has referred, and from which he says nothing will be received, I may say that I have been informed that the steamship companies have made arrangements to occupy these sheds instead of putting up sheds of their own, and the harbour commissioners are satisfied that they will get a revenue of 874,000 a year from that source.
, Mr. MONK. They will never get it.

They say they will, and I believe they will.

I have no doubt the House and the country generally felt a sense of relief when the government promised an investigation into the matter of the concession of the Treadgold grant in the Yukon and other similar hydraulic concessions. But if the House and the public felt any sense of relief at the time that announcement was made by the government, I venture to say that this feeling of relief and satisfaction was superseded by disappointment and even by a shock, when the public and the House read the instructions which were given to the commission which is to be appointed to investigate that matter. I purpose reading extracts from the instructions which were laid upon the Table of the House last Monday, so that I may bring to the minds of the members the utter farce which the government is trying to perpetrate upon the House and the country :
On a report dated 1903, from the Minister of Justice, submitting that for several years placer gold mining has been successfully carried on in the Yukon Territory, particularly in the district

traversed by the Klondike river, and rivers, streams, and creeks tributary thereto.
That only such claims as enjoyed water facilities have heretofore been profitably worked ; that gold is supposed to be distributed in the benches, banks and other elevated grounds along such rivers, streams and creeks.
That owing to the expense and difficulty involved in securing the necessary supply of water the successful prosecution of the industry throughout these last named localities has been seriously retarded and in many cases made impossible ; that it has been represented to the government that great expense is required to be incurred to collect, store and distribute the waters of the said benches, banks and elevated grounds.
That it has also been represented to the government that the extent and value of the deposits of gold in the said benches, creeks and elevated grounds is at present unknown, and must remain so until a sufficient supply of water is available for the construction of hydraulic works, and that parties advancing the moneys for the construction of said works must necessarily take great risks with respect to their investment.
That while it is fitting that reasonable and proper privileges and advantages should te offered which will induee parties to construct such hydraulic works, yet it is essential :
(a.) that no grants or concessions should be made that would interfere with the right to water which any free miner is entitled to under the regulations governing placer mining in the Yukon Territory ;
(b.) that the water so to be held and controlled by the hydraulic companies should be available on equal terms to all free miners whose claims can be profitably worked thereby, and subject to such reasonable rates and conditions to be fixed by the Governor in Ccuncil as shall secure the greatest possible advantage to the district in which the works are established.
That to obtain such hydraulic work and a supply of water for the benches, banks and elevated grounds above mentioned, certain powers, rights and privileges were granted by the Governor General in Council on the 21st of April, 1902, to Malcolm H. Orr-Ewing, A. N. C. Treadgold and Walter Barwick ; that it has been alleged the said grant and concession constitutes a monopoly, which, while depriving the treasury of enormous revenues, is most detrimental to the mining industry of the Yukon.
Now I desire to lay stress upon tills paragraph of instructions, because it is the most important of the whole document. Tt is the part in which the .jurisdiction of the commissioners who are to be appointed is limited, and it is limited simply to the obtaining of information showing to what extent the said concession is likely to be beneficial or injurious to the mining Interests of the said Yukon territory.
That it is very desirable that the commissioners making the inquiry should investigate generally all facts and circumstances which may afford information to the government and to parliament respecting the hydraulic or other means which it is desirable should be adopted [DOT] to successfully develop the benches, banks and other elevated grounds which could only be worked at great disadvantage under natural conditions, or are not able to be profitably Mr. CASGRAIN.
worked at all without an artificial supply of water.
The minister therefore recommends that under the provisions of chapter 114 of the reused statutes of Canada, being an Act entitled an Act respecting inquiries concerning public matters, it be referred-as commissioners to conduct such public inquiry for that purpose, holding the same in Dawson City and elsewhere in the Yukon as they shall determine, the said commissioners to have all the powers of summoning and enforcing the attendance of witnesses, &c.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it will be observed that the only power which is given to these commissioners who are to be appointed is to investigate the scientific problem as to whether or not the hydraulic system is to be introduced into the Yukon Territory for the better carrying out of placer mining in that territory. That is the whole scope of the inquiry. It extends to the Treadgold concession and to other similar concessions, but no further, and also to the obtaining ot information 'respecting the hydraulic or other means which it is desirable should be adopted to' successfully develop the benches, banks and other elevated grounds which could only be worked at great disadvantage under natural conditions.' It will also be observed by the terms of these instructions that the commissioners are to sit in the Yukon Territory only, that is, at Dawson City, or anv other part of the Yukon Territory in which they see fit to sit.
Sir, since this matter was brought before the House some time ago, there is no doubt, and I think hon. gentlemen opposite will not controvert this statement, that there has been a general demand for an inquiry, not only from this side of the House, not only from people who are generally adverse to the present administration politically, but there has been a general demand from all those who have the true interests of the country at heart, that a thorough and complete investigation into all the circumstances surrounding the grant of the Treadgold concession and other hydraulic concessions in the Yukon Territory, should be made. The independent press has been unanimous upon this point, and has asked the government, has demanded from the government, that this investigation should be held. But, Sir, what kind of an investigation ? Not merely an investigation of the scientific questions which are dealt with in the instructions given to the commissioners who are to be appointed, not simply to know whether these hydraulic concessions are to the benefit or the injury of the free miners of the Yukon, but an investigation into all the circumstances surrounding the granting of the Treadgold concession and of other concessions of a similar nature. In a word, I take it that when the question came up before the House the public conscience of this country was shocked at the revelations which were made and brought to the notice of parliament by the reading of the docu-
44S9

meats of which myself and those who followed me in the debate on this side of the House, gave cognizance to this House.
Sir, it was only following up what had taken place in the Yukon itself ; because as I stated, without wishing at all to refer to a prior debate, I brought to the notice of the House the fact that a petition had been presented to this House by the Dawson Board of Trade and by hundreds, yes, by thousands, of the citizens of the Yukon Territory, in which these concessions were denounced in unmeasured terms. I hold in my hand now the petition which was presented to this House on the 16th of April, 1903, by the member of the Yukon. As the House will see, it is a bulky petition, there are many signatures attached to this petition. It was signed by the most prominent citizens of the Yukon, belonging to all shades of political opinion, not only by the adversaries of the government but by those citizens in the Yukon Territory who have at heart the true interests of the Dominion and the pure administration of the affairs of this country. What does this petition say amongst other things ?	.
That the benefits conferred upon the grantees are of incalculable value and involve an enormous exploitation of the public resources of this territory for the benefit of a few favoured concessionaires.
The House will understand what that means. It bore evidence on the face of it to the citizens of the Yukon Territory themselves that this was a grant which was made to certain favourites of the government and that it was an enormous exploitation of the public resources of the Territory to the detriment of the citizens of the Yukon and of the miners. This petition is a most important one because it comes from a public body of the Yukon which has no political leanings and it is signed by thousands of men who must know the condition of affairs in the Yukon and who come to this parliament and ask that an investigation be held into the charges which they make, not only against the concessionaires, but impliedly, also against those who gave these concessions to Treadgold and others.
I also hold in my hand another petition which was presented to the House of Commons from another public body in the Yukon. This is the petition of the corporation of the city of Dawson which is now before the House. It was also presented to this House by the hon. member who represents the Yukon on the 16th of April, 1903, and it contains exactly the same allegation as the petition I have just read; that is the petition of the Dawson Board of Trade. I take it that the condition created by these concessions must be grave indeed when all these citizens come to the House of Commons, call the attention of the House of Commons to these facts and take, as I believe, the unprecedented step of presenting these petitions to the House
and of making these grave charges in the face of the whole country. But, that is not all. If these petitions from the Dawson Board of Trade and from the corporation of the city of Dawson could have been instigated by any political feeling, surely the Liberal Association of Dawson could not have had in its mind any unwarrantable attack upon the administration which it supports. I hold in my hand here the Yukon,'Sun' which is the organ of the Liberal party of the Yukon Territory, and not only that, but, if I turn to page 2 of the issue which I hold in my hand, I find that the Yukon ' Official Gazette ' is the Saturday issue of the ' Sun ' so that it is the official newspaper of the Yukon Territory. According to this paper on the 1st of April last:
At a well attended meeting of the Liberal Club held last night at Pioneer Hall, steps were taken toward strengthening the hand of Mr. Ross, at Ottawa, on several matters of importance to the territory.
Further, a petition is resolved upon and adopted by the Liberal Club of Dawson, friends of hon. gentlemen opposite, then-supporters in the Yukon Territory, and what do we find in this petition ? We find amongst other things this :
Resolved, that an inquiry may be set on foot to ascertain the circumstances under which the leading hydraulic concessions were obtained in order that action may be taken by the Attorney General of Canada in the premises.
That was only following up what happened a few months ago in the Yukon Territory, because, as we all know, an election had taken place at which the hon. member who represents the Yukon Territory (Mr. Ross) was elected, and at that time he was asked very pointedly, in a question which was published in the papers, whether he would take steps to bring to punishment the officials at Ottawa and at Dawson who have given these large concessions to the favourites of the government. He was asked if he would not take the necessary steps to bring these people to punishment for the fraud which they had perpetrated upon the government or which these officials at Ottawa had perpetrated upon the government. We were told to bring specific charges-bring charges against any one, bring charges against any officials, or charges against any minister, bring charges of malfeasance against anybody in authority, make specific charges, say that you will give up your seat if these charges are not proved .and we will grant an immediate inquiry. That is what was thrown out to this side of the House by hon. gentlemen opposite. We have brought to the notice of the House and of the government the charges which are made by these public bodies to which I alluded a minute ago- the Dawson Board of Trade and the corporation of the city of Dawson. We have

brought to the notice of hon. gentlemen opposite the charges made by their own friends in the Yukon, we have laid them before the House and we say now that the government is on its defence and that it should take up these charges. If they are not true it will be good for lion, gentlemen opposite to have an investigation so as to prove that these charges are false and that there is absolutely nothing in them. First of all we were promised an investigation, not an investigation of a scientific character, to ascertain whether or not the government have made a provident bargain by giving these concessions to wash the gold in the Yukon Territory, but we were promised a complete investigation into the charges which had been laid at the door of the government. We were promised this and it was said :	We have not had time yet
to investigate these charges or to appoint commissioners or a committee of this House to investigate them. We are waiting until the hon. member for the Yukon arrives. The navigation is not quite open in the Territory, but wait until navigation is open. Wait until the hon. gentleman takes his seat. I am sorry he is not here. I understand onj very good authority that he will not be here again this session. Wait, and everything that you have said in this House will be investigated by the commissioner :
When the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Ross) returns to Ottawa.-he Is at present in British Columbia. I understand-and we can have the benefit of his advice, it is our intention to fully carry out the representations made to the citizens of the Yukon to have a full investigation into all charges or suspicions that hon. gentlemen may be good enough to mention or entertain in regard to any matters connected with the Yukon administration. I give that public notice to my hon. friend1, so that, in addition to the advantage he has had of ventilating his views on the floor of this House, he will have an opportunity to make good, if he can, any of his charges or suspicions before a tribunal where newspaper extracts and let ters will not be the only evidence, but where gentlemen will have the privilege of pledging their oaths to the truth of all they say.
This was the pledge that was given to this House by the hon. gentleman who spoke for the government when this matter was' brought up. The hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) in reply to the speech which I had the honour to make to the House on the 12th of May last, made a solemn promise to the House and the country that a full and complete Investigation would be held iuto all the charges made at that time against the government, against officials, grantees and concessionaires. I cannot see why the government has changed its mind. We were notified the other day, it is true that the government had come to another conclusion, before these instructions were laid on the Table of the House. We were surprised that it should be given out in the House that the government had recanted, that the * Mr. CASGRAIN.
government had come to another conclusion, that it was not going to grant this full and complete investigation into the charges of fraud which had been laid at its door, but that it was simply going to grant the investigation which is foreshadowed in the instructions to the commissioners which I read a moment ago. At that time the surprise was great. We felt there must be some misapprehension in the mind of the hon. gentleman who was then addressing the House. We could not for a moment believe after that the solemn pledge which had been given to the House in the name of the government by the hon. Postmaster General, that the government would in such a short time change its mind and come to the House, with, as I said before, this farce of an investigation which is going to be confided to Mr. Justice Britton and others. What is the reason of that change of opinion on the part of the hon. ministers who are responsible for the giving of these concessions in the Yukon ? Why do they not now say that they are going to grant a full and complete inquiry into the charges which these people from the Yukon make against the government and the officials who are in charge of this department ?
What has come across the spirit of their dreams ! The natural conclusion and the only conclusion to which this House and the country can come is, that there are guilty parties whom the government is interested in protecting. Here was a minister speaking for the government in this debate and he said on the floor of parliament: you should have known that it has been decided long ago by the government to give a full and complete inquiry into these charges ; we are going to give it as soon as we can and this investigation is going to be so complete that you will have an opportunity of proving all the charges you have made. But when the instructions were brought dowrn we found that the inquiry was limited to the one point as to whether it was provident or improvident on the part of the government to give these concessions in the Yukon Territory. I repeat, and the country will endorse me when I say, that every independent man in this country will come to the conclusion that the only reason why the government is limiting this investigation is because the charges that were made on the 12tli of May in this House, the charges which were made by the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) the other day, are absolutely true, and the government dare not go before a commission even of its own appointment to have these charges investigated, because they are so true that some one on the government benches probably would find these charges so true that he would have to retire from public life.
Hear, hear.

There is noticeable also a change In the manner of the right hon.

the Prime Minister. Compare his conduct now with his conduct in reference to the Drummond County matter. Here are his remarks delivered on February 15tli, 189S- I quote from 'Hansard':
The reasons which compel the government to make this motion will he understood by every one in this House, and I presume also appreciated by everybody. Last year the government undertook to extend the Intercolonial Railway from the present terminus at Chaudidre to Montreal. I am under the impression that this scheme had been engaging the attention of previous governments for some years past. The government selected a route which had the advantage of being, by twenty miles, shorter than the route existing between Ldvis and Montreal over the Grand Trunk Railway and which bad the further merit and advantage of avoiding the chain of mountains which are adjacent to the St. Francis river near Richmond.
I call the attention of the House to this part of my right hon. friend's remarks :
But, suspicious as to the dealings of the government with the company in question-the Drummond Country Railway Company-having been thrown out to the public, the government deem it their duty to court every inquiry and to see that all charges may be properly ventilated.
Here the Prime Minister states that the only reason why the government granted the Drummond County inquiry was because suspicions had been thrown out to the public with regard to the government dealings in the purchase of that railway. There were no specific charges made in this House. We were not defied to make these specific charges, but as the right lion, gentleman says, it was only because suspicions had been thrown out that it was the duty of the government to ask for a full and complete inquiry, and the Prime Minister moved :
That a special committee of the House be appointed to inquire into the expenditure of the subsidies granted by the parliament of Canada in aid of the construction of the Drummond County Railway and into all negotiations rnd transactions between the government of Canada and any member or officer thereof, or any person in its behalf, and the. Drummond County Railway Company, or any director, officer or person in the company's behalf, relating to the acquiring of the siaid railway by the government ; with power to send for papers, persons and records, and to report the evidence to this House, together with the opinion of the said committee thereupon.
How is it that the government has changed its mind now. Why is it that when charges are made by responsible persons in the Yukon, by the Dawson Board of Trade, by the municipal corporation of the city of Dawson. yes, and by even the friends and supporters of the government ; why is it that these charges and these accusations are not to be investigated, while mere suspicions in connection with the Drummond County railway purchase were to be the subject of a full and complete investigation. There is one other reason why the inquiry is limited
to discovering whether Treadgold should have the power to construct hydraulic works in the Yukon, and that one other reason is, that tiie commission is worded in this way in order to throw sand into the eyes of the public. Public opinion demanded a full and complete investigation into everything connected with the transaction, and this kind of investigation is granted so that the government may be able to say : oh, well, we granted an inquiry any way. We well remember how in the first years of this government they used to say to us :	We
will investigate every charge and every accusation you can bring against the government, and not only that, but we will investigate even every suspicion of wrong doing so that the people may know that the men who now sit on the treasury benches compose the purest government that ever held power in Canada. Alas ; how they have changed.
Hear, hear.

Probably the government is growing old and probably a little more wicked than it was in its earlier days, and now we see charges whicji have shocked the public conscience relegated to one side and not investigated. We object to the proposed investigation ; first : because it is too limited in its scope, and second because it is an investigation by a royal commission. What the country demands is a full and complete investigation by a committee of parliament Parliament is in session now and we can have an investigation before a committee of this House. We gave the reason some time ago, why we objected to the appointment of Mr. Justice Britton, and X shall not refer to that again further than to say that tiie independent press of this country unite in beseeching him not to accept the position which the government has offered to him.

The Toronto 'News' is not a journal favouring this side of the House, and it can X believe be called an independent exponent of public opinion. On the 9th instant the Toronto ' News ' wrote :
A Case for Diffidence.
There is no attack, so far as we are aware, upon Mr. Justice Britton as a judge. Not a word has been said in derogation of his impartiality. But it is a thoroughly recognized principle that the best and most impartial judge on the bench should not sit upon a case in which he has had. at any time, a private interest. British practice assumes that in such a case there is a possibility of the most upright men being swayed by an unconscious bias. British scrupulousness has impelled many judges to decline the embarrassment of cases in which their interest was more remote than Judge Britton's in the Yukon case.

That all the words after the word ' that ' be left out, and the following added instead thereof ttfis House regrets that by an Order in Council of date the 21st day of April, 1902, the government, for the ostensible purpose of establishing hydraulic works to supply water for the efficient working of auriferous deposits, have granted to one A. N. C. Treadgold, of London, England, and his associates, vast powers, franchises and concessions in and upon the bends, banks, valleys, slopes and hills of the Klondike river. Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks, and in and upon the waters of Rock creek, in the Yukon Teritory, with the right to establish for the benefit and advantage of the concessionaires, in and through the region and district through which these rivers and creeks run, hydraulic, electrical and other systems, and to enter and to take up and operate mining and other lands.

grievance which the hon. gentleman set up in his motion on the 12th of May. That represented the gravamen of his charge. My hon. friend, with a , great flourish, produces a petition from certain persons. He reads from that petition and suggests that the commission that has been appointed does not cover the case made in this petition. The petition dees not deal with the matters to which my hon. friend refers, provided he read the whole of the petition. This petition, which the hon. gentleman has been kind enough to send me says :
The benefits conferred upon the grantees are of incalculable value, and involve an enormous sacrifice of the resources of this territory for the benefit of a few favoured concessionaires.
I have not read all the petition, but on that point at least, it will hardly be said that it is not covered by the Royal Commission. The Royal Commission, after reciting the Treadgold concession, proceeds to say :
That it is important in the public interest that inquiry be made for the purpose of obtaining information showing to what extent the said grant and concession is likely to be beneficial or injurious to the mining interests of the Yukon Territory.
What is the meaning of that part of the order of reference ? My1 hon. friend- says that the charge is that the concessionaires have obtained great advantage at the expense of the public. The order of reference isi to ascertain whether the grant is likely to be beneficial or injurious to the mining interests of the Yukon Territory. Will any hon. gentleman say that, under that order the charge made in this petition is not fully7 capable of being inquired into ? The order of reference goes on :
That it is also desirable that at the same time the inquiry should not be limited to the said grant and concession, but should extend to all similar concessions granted in the Yukon Territory ;
That it is further desirable that the commissioners making the inquiry should investigate generally all facts and circumstances which may afford information to the government and to parliament respecting the hydraulic or other means which it is desirable should be adopted to successfully develop the benches, banks, and other elevated grounds which can only be worked at great disadvantage under natural conditions or are not able to be worked at all without an artificial supply of water.
So, the point made in this petition is amply covered by the order of reference. But my hon. friend says that an article was read some weeks ago in this House emanating from the Yukon ' Sun,' containing certain charges, and that these are not made a subject of inquiry. I would like to know what would become of parliamentary practice if the charges made in newspapers were to be made the foundation of parliamentary inquiry. My hon. friend cites the case of Mr. Butt, iii which, he says, a member of parliament was able to obtain a parliamentary inquiry" to meet
a charge made against him in an article in the London ' Times.' But where is the charge made against any named person iu any newspaper or by any bon. member of this House ? The hon. gentleman has not dared to name a man. He has made insinuations. If it were parliamentry, I would say that he has assumed a most unworthy part; if I were permitted by the rules to say so 1 would say that he had adopted a cowardly course in making insinuations against members of this House-
Oh, oh.

1 say, Sir, that if it were parliamentary X wouid charge him with having followed a most cowardly procedure in not having named some hon. member instead of insinuating. Let him rise in his place and make a charge against any man and we shall know how to deal with it. But, until he does so, let him not seek a parallel in Mr. Butt's case. In that case, the editor had the manliness to name the member, and the member availed himself of his position to ask for the benefit of an inquiry. Will the hon. gentleman say who is named in this case ? Has he ever named any one ? Does he now name any one ? I will give place to him, if he will rise and name some one in the government or out of the government against who he dare to level a charge. Let him, if he dare, put his honour in the balance with the honour of the man he assails, and we shall see which way the balance will go. But, until he does that, he has not made a case similar to that of Mr. Butt, but has rather put himself in a position which enables him to shelter himself behind the privileges of the House to utter words that will be spread broadcast throughout the country in the hopes that they will spread their poison in fertile ground. Mr. Chairman, the questions resolve themselves into two. The first point is whether there have been improvident grants-whether these concessions have been granted against the public interest. My hon. friend will not say that that branch of the question is not fully covered by the order of reference. Why be so indignant against the appointment of Judge Britton if he is not called upon to deal with the class of charge that my hon. friend shrinks from making but only Insinuates ? If it is merely an inquiry into the business phase of the question, the personality of the commissioner is not of such special importance. If, however, the charge were of a different character then, perhaps, my hon. friend would have some force in his contention that, according to the form of the charge the inquiry might be before a different tribunal-perhaps, before a committee of the House. But, up to this moment, the hon. gentleman has not ventured to suggest anything that would commit him to the truthfulness or belief in the truthful-

ness or otherwise of any accusation. He simply alludes to the business phase of the question, shirking carefully any personal responsibility as to the accusations he has made. Now, 1 ask, Mr. Chairman, is it fair for the hon. gentleman to act in that way ? Is it fair toward the country for him to make use of his position as a member of this House to make insinuation, and yet, at the same time, to shrink from the responsibility of making charges V Other members of this House in days gone by have, at different times, had the courage of their suspicions. But not so on this occasion. And yet my hon. friend seeks to add to his motion of the 12th of May, by pretending that it asked for more than it did, and endeavours to make out that the House is bound to do more than he asked for on that occasion, because, at a subsequent date, I made a statement, whieh, lie says, would carry the inquiry beyond the limit to which it is at present confined. What were the circumstances under which I made the statement ? My hon. friend was well aware that Mr. Ross, the hon. member for the Yukon is more or less familiar with the conditions of the Yukon, and more or less familiar with the state of public opinion in that district. He is aware that this question became a political question during the election in the Yukon, and the people there naturally look to Mr. Ross, as their representative, to take a more or less active part in dealing with matters that interest them. Therefore, when this question came before the House, at the time it did, it seemed to me inopportune that we should finally dispose of the case in the absence' of the hon. member for'the Yukon. At that time the member for the Yukon was not in his place in parliament. Every one knows that he has sustained a great bereavement and that his health broke down under the sad affliction, and although he hoped to be able to attend the session, yet his health has obliged him to absent himself. When this matter came before the House the government had no opportunity of consulting with him, we did not know his precise whereabouts, he was in the west moving about for his health. I think at the moment he was in British Columbia, and it was some time before I found out his whereabouts. But I stated in the House that when Mr. Ross came to Ottawa and we had an opportunity of consulting with him with regard to all the matters of the Yukon, we would issue a commission of inquiry of the character to which I referred. I have not yet seen Mr. Ross, he has not yet been to Ottawa, I trust his health will enable him to come here; but up to this moment we have not had an opportunity of seeing him, and therefore the inquiry which was proposed to be undertaken must be deferred until his arrival.

same statement I made, I then suggested that the inquiry would be as extensive as the hon. gentleman's charges, and if it were limited to his charges at this moment, certainly it would not be a very extensive inquiry. Why, Sir, I would ask the hon. gentleman what is the nature of the inquiry that is to be made ? He is a member of the bar. I shall advocate the reduction of fees, which,

And my hon. friend from Montmorency standing in his place here to-night is only adopting the platform of Mr. Ross the member for the Yukon in asking the government to have a full inquiry.
Hear, hear.

Let the Postmaster General bear that in mind before he attempts to taunt my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) in the weak and .unworthy manner in which he has attempted to taunt him to-night.

Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, bear.

The member for the Yukon says 1 I will advocate a thorough investigation of these frauds,' and a few days ago the Postmaster General speaking perhaps a little hastily as he sometimes does, but speaking candidly said :
I would also state to my hon. friend who tells us that he is very desirous of investigation, that I am sure he must well know that it has long been the fixed intention of the government to hold such an investigation.
How was my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) to know it. He was only to know it from the fact that the member from the Yukon, elected as a supporter of this government had promised his electors that' lie would obtain for them a thorough investigation into these very charges of fraud which were brought to the attention of the House tonight by the hon. gentleman from Montmorency.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend the Postmaster General continued :
The hon. gentleman must remember that when the election was held, promises were given to the people of the Yukon that there would be a commission to inquire into the whole administration of that territory.
And in what language was that promise given. Let me read once more.
A thorough investigation of the charges of fraud made in respect to the manner in which certain concessions are alleged to have been obtained, and if such fraud is established the immediate commencement of such proceedings as may be required to vacate the grants.
That beyond doubt is the language to which the Postmaster General was alluding, and the platform of the hon. member for the Yukon is the only source from which the hon. member for Montmorency could have obtained the knowledge which was attributed to him by the Postmaster General. But the Postmaster General taunts the hon. member for Montmorency and he says : Name your names and give us something more than mere rumours. I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman who leads the House, and the hon. Postmaster General, to show me the names that were given in the resolution moved by the right hon. gentleman with regard to the Drummond County Rail-wav. I pause to ask either one of these hon. gentlemen to show me one single line in that resolution giving the name of any individual. And yet the right hon. gentleman, on that occasion, adopting a course very different from that which he asks the hon. Postmaster General to defend to-night, said :
The reasons which compel the government to make this motion will be understood by every one in this House. Suspicions as to the dealings of the government with the company Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
in question, the Drummond County Railway Company, having been thrown out to the public, the government deem it their duty to court every inquiry, and to see that all charges may be properly ventilated.
Well, why do the government not deem it their duty now, when the platform of their own candidate in the Yukon demanded that these charges should be investigated, why do they not deem it their duty to court every inquiry, and why does my hon. friend the Postmaster General stand up in this House and say : Name me some names, and I will give you the inquiry ? What is the difference ? Having regard to the platform of their own candidate, having regard to the charges of the Liberal clubs, having regard to the charges put forward by the board of trade and the corporation of the city of Dawson, there is tenfold more reason why the government should on this occasion court inquiry than there was on the occasion on which my right hon. friend stood up in this House and, amid the applause of his followers, said : The government deem it their duty to court every inquiry, suspicions having been thrown out to the public ; and the same hon. gentlemen who hailed that announcement with applause sit in their seats to-night and hail with applause the announcement of the hon. Postmaster General that the government not only do not court any inquiry, but will not grant any inquiry unless names are named. I leave the hon. gentlemen to their own position in that respect ; but the public of Canada will not. I think, be slow to appreciate the difference in the attitude of the government on that occasion, when the right hon. gentleman thought it his duty to court inquiry, and on this occasion, when the hon. Postmaster General, having spoken for the Crown and having promised a thorough Investigation of every subject, stands up and says that he has fulfilled every obligation to the people of this country by granting a mere investigation as to whether or not the concession granted to Mr. Treadgold and his associates was a provident or improvident concession. Take the resolution of my hon. friend from Montmorency, read that resolution from beginning to end. and point out if you can one single word in it that is not justified by the facts. My hon. friend the Postmaster General did not attempt to do that. He contented himself with standing up in this House and throwing a few weak taunts at my hon. friend from Montmorency ; and then, notwithstanding the platform on which his candidate was elected, notwithstanding his own direct reference to that platform a few weeks ago. notwithstanding his deliberate promise to this House, speaking, as he did. for the government, he has the audacity now to say that this government have fulfilled every pledge and every duty to the House and the country by granting this ineffectual commission.

Now, Mr. Speaker, it .may be possible for the government, with the aid of their followers, to vote down this motion ; bnt all I have to say is that in doing so they are departing from their own direct pledge, conveyed to the House and the country through the hon. Postmaster General, and they are departing from the promise made by their own candidate to the electorate of the Yukon, upon which he obtained his election to this House, and upon which his election was hailed as a Liberal victory. If my right hon. friend and his colleagues are satisfied with the contrast their conduct on this occasion presents to the attitude of my right hon. friend when he moved for the inquiry with regard to the Drummond County Hailway, we shall leave them to their satisfaction ; but when the country comes to pass judgment on this matter, i do not think that it will be so easily satisfied as are the members of the government and those who support them in this House.

Mr. Speaker, I think that any deliberate or calm-minded individual who may be present and hear this discussion, will feel rather compelled to the conclusion that our hon. friends opposite are endeavouring, by the violence of their language and the apparent intensity of their feelings, to make up for an exceedingly weak case-for a dearth of material and a lack of facts to fit the accusations which they are making against the government. My hon. friend starts out with intimating that in the proposal which the government has made for an inquiry into this Yukon matter, we are simply showing what an utter farce the thing has developed into, because we have limited the scope of the inquiry to the questions of hydraulic mining and the character of the country from the hydraulic mining point of view. If this is such an iniquitous farce as the hon. gentleman chooses to characterize it, then all the more readily is it capable of being proved that it is a farce, that we are not covering the ground which the public interests require us to cover, and that we are not going the length we ought to go in the investigation which we are to make. I take my hon. friend's resolution, and I am prepared to follow the various clauses and statements contained in it; and I take it that my hon. friend has put forward the very best case he can ; that he has alleged the strongest possible facts ; that he has summoned to his assistance all that his ingenuity would suggest in the framing of the resolution, to lead up to the conclusion which he asks the House to draw, and which he has himself drawn, namely, that the proposal of the government is nothing but an iniquitous farce. My hon. friend says in this resolution :
For some time the grants by the government of Canada to certain parties, and, among others, 142
to A. N. C. Treadgold and his associates, of hydraulic concessions in the Yukon Territory, have been publicly denounced as fraudulent :
That at a convention held in the city of Dawson, on or about the 1st of October, 1902, for the purpose of selecting a Liberal candidate to represent the Yukon Territory in this parliament of Canada, it was, among other things, resolved, that many of the concessions above mentioned were obtained by fraud and imposition.	.
Now, I ask my hon. friends calmly, if they can summon enough calmness for the purpose, to consider what this language means. Does not the hon. gentleman who moves this resolution feel in his own mind and conscience-if he does not, he ought to feel it that what these people were complaining of was not fraud perpetrated by the government or to which the government was a party, but some fraudulent representations and impositions that had been practiced on the officers of the department and that had induced them to grant this Tread-gold concession. Is there any warrant or justification for drawing from the language which the hon. gentleman has used in his resolution, and which is a counterpart of what is found in newspaper statements and in various other forms made by the Yukon people, the inference that there is any personal or political implication or accusation involved in it against the government or any member of the administration ? Is it not all that can be fairly implied from the language which the hon. gentleman puts forward, that there have been persons who, in procuring these concessions, practiced fraud and imposition upon the government or the officials acting for the government ? A fair reading of the clauses which the hon. gentleman has embodied in his own motion can bring one's mind to no other conclusion. If I am right in this, what foundation is there for the hon. gentleman to say that there is the slightest warrant in anything contained in these two clauses for saying that there is such a prima facie case established as would justify this government in treating these statements as reflecting upon the government or any member of it ? We know how easy it is in a country such as the Yukon, filled with all sorts of people, adventurers from all countries of the world, to create excitement of any kind. These people, so far removed from the control of government, and hoping to achieve great things in their thirst for the precious metals, feel as though they own the country, and had the right to distribute it among themselves. Such a class of people would not stop to consider what was best in the general interest or whether or not this policy or the other would not be more advantageous in the future. But would only look to their own immediate selfish interests. They would not be disposed to listen to reason, but would want to lay their hands on everything in sight, regardless of whether or not the results would be disastrous to the future



*welfare and interests of tire country. In that frame of mind, when the government had decided, after due consideration, that it was in the best interest of the country to establish a system of hydraulic mining upon a large scale and conducted on the most modern mechanical methods, they did not pause to consider whether or not the mesjns which the government adopted would not in the long run be better for them, but determined to see in it only an obstacle in their way, and started this wild excitement. Under the influence of that excitement, therefore, they gave vent to these exaggerated statements and jumped to the conclusion that, because a concession had been granted, there must necessarily have been fraud and misrepresentation practiced on the government. I think that if a jury of non-partisans were summoned to consider the effect of the language used by these people, and if the jury brought its mind to bear on the conditions existing in the Yukon and the class of men gathered there and who created this excitement, they would be driven to the conclusion that the language used did not in any sense involve any reflection or imputation on the integrity of that government or any of its members.
The amendment goes on to deal with the representative of the Yukon :
That James Hamilton Ross, Esquire, now a member for this House for the Yukon Territory in accepting the nomination offered to him by the said convention promised publicly through the press to advocate a thorough ^ investigation of the charges of fraud aforesaid.
That I do not dispute. I dare say that Mr. Ross himself, although I do not know it as a matter of fact, may have been carried off his feet by that furious craze which had seized the people amongst whom this hydraulic system was going to be established. I could understand that my hon. friends opposite, cool-headed as they usually are when they see no political advantage to be gained, might, if they had been out in the Yukon, have been affected by the same wave of excitement. Everybody was at the moment carried away by it. They would not have paused to consider more than anybody else, but it devolves on this parliament to consider whether it is consistent with Its dignity to appoint a commission in order that somebody may be subjected to inquiry to find out what that somebody did. If there had been practiced, as these people imagine- *and as I am willing to admit, in this excited state of mind, they believed fraud and misrepresentation on the government, by means of which these privileges were granted, there will still be no necessity to grant a parliamentary commission. The law furnishes adequate means of getting at the facts. If anybody believed that fraud and misrepresentation had been practiced, he could appeal to the courts or [DOT]to the department. All he has to do is Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
to appeal to the department to have an inquiry, and he would be afforded every opportunity by the department of making his *charges good. The law also affords a remedy.
