If the department refused to grant an investigation, he could take out a writ of scire facias, be given every opportunity to establish before the courts whether such fraud or misrepresentation had been practiced as would invalidate the grant. The court would have discretion to set aside the grant, and the person who claimed that he ought to get it and was unjustly deprived of the privilege of getting it, would have the course open to him to secure it. It is a case essentially to be dealt with by the court and not by a parliamentary committee. You do not want to take a sledgehammer to break an egg. All you need do is to appeal to the proper quarter in the proper way, stating a sufficient case to enable tbe minister to judge whether, in his discretion, he should recommend that the expenditure be incurred, and you have all the remedy you could possibly ask.
Now, we come to the next clause of my hon. friend's indictment, or statement of the facts on which he relies :
That the Board of Trade of the city of Dawson and others on the 16th of April, 1903, presented to this House a petition in which it is alleged that the said concessions to A. N. C. Treadgold and his associates ' involved an enormous exploitation of the public resources of this territory, for the benefit of a few favoured concessionaires.
Now, what does that mean ? Is not that simply an expression of the dissatisfaction of the board of trade, they being impressed, as the other people there are, with the idea that the system that the government has adopted would do injury to the country? I am prepared to admit that they were so impressed. But, that being the case, is this anything more than an expression of discontent with the adoption of this policy ? ' Involving an enormous exploitation of the public resources of this country '-is that anything more than to say that the policy of the government is most disastrous to the interests of that section of the Dominion ? Where is the imputation there that would reflect on the integrity of a minister of the Crown ? Where is the warrant there, or in any statement the hon. gentleman has made, that would justify the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) in rising in his place, having the responsibility of a member of parliament, and saying that he declines to take the responsibility of incriminating a member of parliament or a minister of the Crown who is not able, at present, to be in his seat in this House ? What is there in this amendment, from the beginning to the end of it, that would warrant any member of this House who has the slightest sense of the responsibility attaching to his position in making such an imputation as that ? I have no doubt-I re-

peat it-on the contrary 1 freely confess, that the people in the Yukon, whether you take the board of trade, the common council or any other organization or portion of the inhabitants, are deeply impressed with the idea that if you have these Treadgold concessionaires or any others operating this hydraulic system according to the only way in which it can be worked, you are going to deprive the people of advantages and privileges that they would otherwise individually enjoy, and so do injury to the country. But, that is a mere question of opinion. Would anybody be willing to allow the people in one portion of Canada, particularly a section filled with valuable minerals from which we expect to be able by adopting wise, modern, up-to-date methods to extract great values-would he allow those people to compel the working of these mineral deposits by the individual methods pursued in other times ? Would anybody say that the people directly interested and concerned are the proper people to form a judgment as to the best methods by which these important questions in that country should be dealt with ? Would anybody be warranted in saying that ? We are not taking this step unadvisedly or without precedent. We are not adopting a system which has not been adopted elsewhere and used with success. We could point to dozens of places in the hill countries of the United States where these hydraulic methods had been adopted. And you cannot put two companies one alongside the other, to work the same territory. As I said the other day, when speaking of this matter, the method must be monopolistic or you cannot work it at all. These people complain because this is a monopoly. But how can you erect dams, accumulate water, and arrange for letting this water down to the lower levels to be used in connection with the work of mining, unless you have one organization and one management to control the whole matter-subject, of course, to proper government supervision ? There is no alternative, except to leave things as they are. If there was any fault to be found with the terms under which this concession was granted, then, the government must submit to criticism as to those terms. But this is a question of policy. Can any man say that this government would be worthy of the place it occupies, would it be fit to manage the affairs of this country if, after having studied the question and considered the experience in other places, they were puerilely to do nothing and refuse to adopt the policy which is the only one from which the best results could be obtained ? We would be open to the strongest condemnation if we declined to do what we did-always provided, of course, that the work is carried out by proper methods. If you read these clamorous complaints from beginning to end, you find little in them but an attack 1424
on the government policy. Therefore, I say, you are obliged, if you wish to be fair, not to take as conclusive the judgment of the people who have every interest, as they feel -I think mistakenly-that if they had their own way it would bring to them the best results. Dismiss from these clamorous complaints the idea that the monopoly itself is an evil, that it is an exploitation of individual rights, and you have absolutely nothing with which to deal. We are told that the board of trade made the complaint to which I have alluded. Granted. We are told that on or about the 23rd March, the corporation of the city of Dawson addressed to the House a petition similar in terms to the petition of the board of trade. Granted. The observations which I have made, as to the petition of the board of trade, if those observations at all commend themselves to the House, apply with the same force to the petition of the corporation of the city of Dawson. Then, in the next clause we are told that the Liberal Association of Dawson publicly denounced the said concession as having been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation. What does that mean ? Does that not mean exactly what the second clause of the amendment means as I have explained it ? It means that persons outside, interested in obtaining these concessions, used fraud and misrepresentation, and by these means secured the issue of these grants. I claim the right to conclude from this clause, as from the other, that there is nothing to warrant any suspicion that the integrity of a minister of the Crown is in the slightest degree impeached by the statements made. My hon. friend's motion goes on :
That on the 12th day of May last the government by the honourable, the Postmaster General, during the debate on the Treadgold Concession. promised to this House to fully carry out the representations which had been made to the citizens of the Yukon to have a full investigation into all charges or suspicions that could be mentioned or entertained in regard to any matters connected with the Yukon administration.
I have, therefore, passed in review, perhaps, somewhat at length, all the clauses of this amendment which the hon. gentleman has placed one on top of the other, endeavouring to construct a superstructure which would prove that there had beeu charges made against the government, or involving the character and integrity of a minister of the Crown, I claim to have shown that the hon. gentleman has failed in his purpose, for that is manifestly the purpose which he had in view. He has correctly enough quoted wbat has been said in these speeches and newspapers and other documents. But. taking all these, and assuming, for the sake of argument, the the construction which is put upon them by the hon. gentlemen opposite, what do they lead to ? In substance, as they interpret

them, they are a statement that charges of fraud have been made against the government in granting this concession. Now we are invited, upon that assumption, that unwarrantable assumption, to name a parliamentary committee. To do what ? The hon. gentleman says, to investigate the charges. I will tell you what you are inviting the government to appoint a parliamentary committee to do. It is to sit down and find out what it is that is charged against the government. You have not told us what the government is charged with. You are simply saying that there was fraud in the granting of this concession, and that therefore a committee should be appointed. Now, could any committee which this House might appoint sit down to discharge its functions without trying, in the first place, to discover what it is of which this fraud consisted ? The most rudimentary ideas of parliamentary government would compel hon. gentlemen opposite to tell the House and the country what are the facts which they think constitute a fraud in the transaction of which the government is guilty. Is it not reasonable that such a demand as that should be made upon hon. gentlemen opposite before they ask this House to vote a parliamentary committee ? We have only a wild, indefinite, vague statement that there was fraud in granting the concession, a statement made by somebody, a statement of which no member of parliament will assume the responsibility of vouching for, or of saying he believes it. I say, Mr. Speaker, as I have said once before in speaking upon this subject, that the parliament of Canada would be placing itself in a very ridiculous position if it took any such course.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier stated, and the hon. member for Montmorency has stated, that we are taking to-day, i.i reference to this matter, a very different attitude from what we have taken hitherto ; and he says that in the early life of this government, when vague and general statements were made, based on mere suspicions entertained by hon. gentlemen opposite, this government hastened to meet those statements and declared that they were ready, nay, anxious to have them inquired into. Well, Sir, I do not remember that any circumstance occurred in connection with the Drummond County Railway matter of a vague and non-specific character such as the hon. gentleman says exist in the present instance. I happen to remember something about that case, and I know that in the Drummond County Railway matter there was more than a sweeping charge of wrongdoing by the government. That is not said here, but it was said in that case. Now. I am prepared to accept the challenge which the hon. leader of the opposition made to this side of the House a short time ago when he asked us to name a single specific statement. I have not had time to look through the * Hansard ' for the purpose of giving all the statements that were made by Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to the Drummond Railway transaction, I am unable to do that in the time at my disposal. I remember very well that one member of this House then, now dead, made the very nastiest kind of imputations in respect to the Drummond County transaction ; I remember that the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals relieved himself on two or three different occasions of reflections upon the conduct of the present minister in that transaction. But after the committee had reported, and after the investigation had resulted in total and absolute failure, then they hastened to say that they had never made any imputation against the government or any member of it which would involve their integrity, but they had simply impeached the prudence of the arrangement, and the business character of the arrangement. They told us that after the thing wns over, and their efforts had proved futile. Now I have here the speech which was made by the hon. member for Montmorency upon one occasion, and how often he made it. I have not been able to ascertain. But any one reading this will agree that there was matter of a specific character to justify any minister in claiming an inquiry and investigation, and that it was not of such a nature, emanating from the quarter it did, that it should be disregarded. The language I am going to quote will be found in the ' Hansard ' of 1808, volume 1. page 514.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: That was after the premier had announced that this committee would be appointed.

Yes, it was on the 15th of February, I think it was before the commission was actually appointed, but after the statement was made that it would be appointed. You will see what the hon. gentleman then said, and I think the inference may fairly be drawn that if the hon. member, after he had got his committee, would make a statement of this kind, he would be not unlikely to make even stronger statements, statements that would secure the appointment of a committee which he might think, upon investigation, would disclose something of which he had no evidence, but which was matter of suspicion with him. He said :
But what, above all, was it that made this investigation necessary ? It was the extraordinary speech made in this House last session by the Minister of Public Works. Why, Sir, charged, as he was, in the public press with being interested in the deal he rose in this House and said that ' La Patrie ' newspaper, in which he writes every day, which is his organ, which, if report is true-I do not know whether it is true or not, and I do not state it as a fact- virtually belongs to him, was bought for his sons with a cheque for $30,000 furnished by the president of the Drummond Cdunty Railway.
Now, the hon. gentleman could not put that statement upon the ' Hansard ' and cir-

culate it through the country except for the purpose of creating the impression in the public mind that there was a bargain arising out of this Drummond County business, under which $30,000 passed from the president of the Drummond County Railway into the hands of the Minister of Public Works as a consideration for the transaction. He would not make the statement with any other design in view than to asperse and besmirch the character of the minister to whom he referred. If he did it then-and he did it-how was it possible for the Minister of Public Works otherwise than to say : You have made statements, and members of the House of Commons have made statements of that kind, and therefore I hail with pleasure an investigation into the matter in order that all the facts shall be brought out. But now, has there been a word said, except by insinuation, by the hon. gentleman indicating what the character or nature of the conduct was which he said was attributed by public rumour to a minister of the Crown? Not a syllable. There is nothing to take hold of, and there is nothing which any self-respecting parliament could regard as emanating from a responsible quarter involving such a reflection upon a minister of the Crown as would even leave that minister of the Crown, innocent as he might be and innocent as he is in the present case, the victim of the rumours which are always freely circulated by-I will not say members of parliament- but freely circulated by partisans of one side or the other to the disparagement of their opponents. Under such circumstances, in the face of such a lack of specific material, in the absence of any statement of fact which would show that there had been fraud or malfeasance in office committed by any minister of the Crown or by the government, I cannot see how it would be possible for this government to maintain a position of self-respect if we were to allow hon. gentlemen opposite to obtain a committee of this House to hold an investigation. The government has not changed its mind. I am not conscious that there is present on the treasury benches any member of the administration who would wish to treat questions, reflections, accusations, imputations or insinuations of that kind any differently to-day from the way in which he would wish to treat them two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven years ago. There is only one thing that I can imagine would influence the mind of a minister to-day. If the government had treated seriously some of the scandalous rumours which had been aired by hon. gentlemen opposite reflecting upon the government, if we had held investigations, and if our experience of such charges was that there was not a particle of foundation for them, we might very well hesitate when the same sort of procedure was again committed. But we have once, twice or three times allowed
ourselves to assume that what has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite was entitled to be treated seriously and entitled to be treated with consideration. We have found, having acted under that impression, that we were deceived as to the knowledge that these hon. gentlemen possessed, or as to the foundation upon which they based these imputations, and having had the experience which we have had of the methods of procedure adopted by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, we will no longer continue to follow that course, but will ask and demand and require of these hon. gentlemen that they shall take the responsibility, if they want to reflect unfavourably upon the character of a minister of the Crown, of expressing the opinion that there is reason for the imputations which they have made, and we will demand that they shall take this responsibility manfully and honourably before the House. It is infinitely more to the credit of a member of parliament, who, believing these charges which have been talked about and rumoured in the country in regard to malfeasance or misconduct of the members of the government, should find out afterwards that he was mistaken in his belief, than that he should insinuate and impute misconduct, or that he should avail himself of the position which the people have placed him in to disseminate broadcast over the Dominion reflections upon the character of men who are filling ministerial positions. I do not care what party is in or who are members of the administration ; for the time being the people have entrusted them with the responsibility of carrying on their affairs. For the time being they hold the distinguished and honourable positions of ministers, they possess the confidence of the people, and, representing the people, I think it is at least the duty of those who oppose their policy to recognize that they are in the positions which they fill by the voice of the people of Canada, and as such they are entitled to be treated with that respect which the choice of the people of Canada merits.
I therefore claim that there is nothing alleged in the amendment which the hon. gentleman has moved, that there is notiling which has been stated in support of that amendment to justify this House in departing from the usual practice which obtains under ail parliamentary governments through the various portions of the empire, and that there is no course remaining for us but to give a decided negative to the amendment which the hon. gentleman has proposed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext:
Mi-. Speaker, I crave your indulgence for a very short statement that I feel it is my duty to offer. I was a member of the government when this Treadgold concession was granted. It came up in the ordinary

way of business. The matter lay within the department of the Interior. All those who have been ministers know that the minister who has charge of a department brings before his colleagues matters that are under his control. That matter, as a matter of course, was presented to the government by the minister then in charge of the Department of the Interior. The matter was discussed with all the care and attention that we were able to give to it then. We looked into the question to the best of our ability. It was referred to a sub-committee. One of the members of this sub-committee is no more a member of this parliament. The concession was granted after, as I said, we had given our best attention to the question. It was a difficult question, as my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) has said, when we were called upon to decide whether it was better to leave things as they were, to leave the miners to supply themselves with water, or whether it would be better to grant certain rights to parties who wrere undertaking to supply water under certain conditions. The first conditions that we imposed upon them were not carried out. They came to us later on and reported that they could not go on with their undertaking unless these conditions were changed. I think there were three changes. However, this has no great bearing on the case. So far as my own standpoint is concerned, all I can say is that I do not know that there is any one of my colleagues in the House to-night who was my colleague then, who I am sure has been guilty of an impropriety. As far as I can see. there is no member of this government within the preeincts of this hall-
Hear, hear.

Well, I do not want my words to be misinterpreted. I am just going to explain what I mean. I do not want that my words be interpreted in a wider direction than I want to give them. I generally endeavour to speak my mind very clearly. Then I understand the hot words that my hon. friend the Postmaster General has used. He is not guilty I am sure of any impropriety; he has resented the accusation that has been made against the government and I cannot blame him for that. Speaking for myself I know that as far as I have been able to judge the matter has come before us in the ordinary way of business. Eight or ten months afterwards or perhaps a little less, a deputaion came to us to Ottawa. It was headed by Mr. Ross, who represents the Yukon in this parliament. Complaints were made that the concessions were too wide; that the concessions in point of fact should be cancelled or at any rate amended in such a way that they would not be the same thing at all. The matter was taken into consideration and the changes were made. Now, this is all I have got to say Hon. Mr. TARTE.
so far as the members of the government present to-day are concerned. Let me express my regret that the hon. Minister of the Interior and Mr. Ross are not here. I trust that if the Minister of the Interior were here, after the words that have been uttered by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) he would take the position that I have taken myself in that famous celebrated and notorious inquiry of the Drummond County Railway. In 1897, there were vague accusations in that Drummond County matter. No direct accusations were made, hut having read and heard these vague rumours, I got up in my place and I challenged any direct accusation against me. These accusations did not materialize. Let me tell my hon. friends on the other side of the House, now that they are looking to the wrong pew.
gome hon. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

What did take place during the recess between 1897 and 1898 ? The hon. Mr. Foster, the ex-Minister of Finance, went to Toronto and addressed a large meeting in which my name and the names of my sons were mentioned. When parliament was convened in 1898 I made it a duty to ask the Prime Minister and my colleagues, to themselves ask for an investigation.
Hear, hear.

I would not allow the government of which I was a member to lie under the accusation that had been made against me outside of the chamber, but by a gentleman who had been a minister of the Crown. I thought that that accusation had been enough for me to go to the Prime Minister and to say that if I was guilty of having received directly or indirectly $30,000 in that Drummond County deal I was not worthy to be a member of the government any longer. That is the position I took. No direct accusation has been made against the Minister of the Interior to-day. Rumours have been circulated this evening. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has quoted these rumours without naming the minister but naming his department. I have no doubt-I hope at any rate that if the hon. gentleman who is the Minister of the Interior were here he would take the position that I now take. I shall not vote on this motion and I will tell you why, Sir. In view of the vagueness of the accusation I think that the government would have been justified in declining an inquiry. When there are questions of fraud directly or indirectly mentioned it is necessary; it is proper at any rate to be direct as the rules of parliament require. But the government has granted an inquiry. I was not able to be here when the first motion was discussed, but had I been here I would have spoken just as I speak now. The government have

granted an inquiry. In my humble opinion they hare not acted as they might have acted had they paused a little more. An inquiry by a judge is always a doubtful thing. Some years ago I condemned in the press as a newspaper man, inquiries conducted by judges. It is a dangerous thing to involve the judiciary in such an inquiry as a rule. I do not say that there are not exceptions, but as a rule, parliament should keep the control of its own affairs. It is the safest rule. My hon. friends on the treasury benches have not followed that rule and they have thought proper to appoint a judge. I cannot approve of their action on that account. On the other hand in view of the fact that X have been a member of the government, that I have participated in the granting of the concession that the government is defending to-night, I cannot possibly condemn myself in voting for the motion which implies the condemnation of a transaction to which I have been a party. So far as I know it officially, as it came before us officially, I do not know of anything upon which I could base my judgment to condemn now what I have approved and participated in then. But not approving the procedure that my hon. friends on the treasury benches have adopted, I cannot vote with them.

Mr. Speaker, I was so impressed by the eloquence and convinced by the logic of the Minister of Railways and Canals, that I have no hesitation in saying that if any hon. gentleman on this side of the House-no, I will withdraw that and apologize for it- if any benighted Tory between the Atlantic and the Pacific should be so bereft of his faculties as to suggest the case that the Minister of Railways and Canals so successfully controverted to-night, I would be ready to join with him in taking the proper means to have this irresponsible lunatic at once put under restraint. May I be pardoned before discussing the. question, if I refer to the statement of the Minister of Railways and Canals. He read the motion at present before the House; he read it carefully, clause by clause, so far as the clause charges were concerned, and he found that the sum total of these charges was that the people of the Yukon, irrespective of party, of politics, of creed or anything else; the board of trade, the citizens in public meeting, the Liberal association, everybody in fact had agreed that the government had been imposed upon, and that these concessions had been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation; but the Minister of Railways and Canals nailed his flag at the mast and said :	We deny
there is any charge there of dishonesty on the part of the government. Who said there was ? But are the hon. gentlemen occupying the treasury benches more than demigods; have they eaten the fruit of the tree of knowledge; is it not possible that they
may have been deceived ? And if these-charges be true-and all that is asked on this side of the House is that they be investigated to see whether or not they are true- if it be the fact that the hon. gentlemen opposite, despite all their ability and honesty and integrity-and nobody is accusing them on any of those points-have been deceived, and that these concessions have been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation; can anybody say that we, sitting here as representatives of the people, are doing other than our duty in asking for an investigation, in order to see if the government has been deceived, and if they have been induced by fraud and misrepresentation to make concessions which everybody in the Yukon says are ruinous to that part of the country ? The question seems a simple question, and one would imagine that it would not require any great amount of oratory or discussion to decide it. I think my hon. friend the Postmaster General put the matter in a nutshell when he said that there had been a cowardly course taken and honour was in the balance. I am inclined to agree with him, and the question before us this evening is, who has taken the cowardly course, and whose honour is in the balance ?
A reference to the undisputed facts of the case would furnish, I submit, a complete answer to these questions. It will be admitted that a few years ago the people of this country were possessed of a valuable domain in the Yukon. It will be admitted that by Order in Council, which is wholly invalid-because the hon. Postmaster General himself admitted it the other night- those lands were made over, without one single dollar being paid for them, to a few concessionaires. It is true, as I said, that the hon. gentleman says the Order in Council is invalid; but this House and the unfortunate people of this country have had experience before this of another invalid Order in Council. It was but a few years ago when we learned to our sorrow that a minister of the Crown-and the same minister who is in charge of the Interior Department which controls the Yukon-some seven or eight days before parliament met, rushed through an Order in Council authorizing a railway to be constructed into this very country. It is perfectly true, the order was hopelessly and helplessly invalid; and it is equally true that this unfortunate country paid over $300,000 on the strength of that helplessly invalid Order in Council. And so, Sir, it is perhaps not surprising that the people of the Yukon, excitable as the hon. Minister of Railways says they were, living on the spot, and finding all their hopes of that country blasted, declared in resolution after resolution that the concessions which were granted would mean that in a few years there would be in that country one Treadgold and several hundred people working for him. It is no wonder that

they asked this parliament to investigate the grounds on which these extraordinary concessions were given. It is all very well for the hon. Minister of Railways to say that they are an excitable people. Who are those people ? The Board of Trade of Dawson; a public meeting convened in Dawson ; aye, Sir, the Liberal Association of Dawson ; aye, Sir, the representative of the people sent from Dawson. And so we find that the people of that country, whom we represent, and the right hon. gentleman who leads the government, the Postmaster General sitting beside him, and the Minister of Railways represent these people as much as they represent the people of their own constituencies-these people are to be called an excitable people because, feeling that everything worth anything in their country has been given away, they protested and charged the government, not with fraud, but with being imposed upon, and therefore asked their trustees, who are sent here to transact their business, simply to look into the matter and see if they had not been imposed upon, and if so, to cancel these iniquitous concessions. If we are taunted that we cannot find precedents in English history to meet a case like this, the answer is not far afield. No one can read of cases in which members of the British parliament have resigned thfiir seats without appreciating the fact that the sense of honour is so sensitive there that even if these charges were made, as they have been, by public meetings, by resolutions, by newspapers in the Yukon, there would be not only an investigation, but a vacant seat behind the right hon. leader of the government long before this. But admitting, that the country owned certain lands in the Yukon, and that those lands were given away, though by an Order in Council which is invalid on its face; admitting that the people in the part of the country protested against this; we find that an election was held in that country; and we have been taunted by the hon. Postmaster General that it is idle for us to ask for any investigation into the affairs of the Yukon because the people of that country, in sending to this House a supporter of the government, had shown their confidence in the government which had passed these extraordinary concessions. If the right hon. leader of the government would read the platform of the Liberal Association of the Yukon, which I will not occupy the time of the House in reading, as it has been read already, he would find that it condemned these concessions as strongly as any Conservative member of this House could; and if he would look at the questions wl;ich were asked of the candidate, and answered, not by that gentleman, because he was absent from the country, but by a gentleman high in his confidence, who conducted the election for him-a gentleman in whom the right hon. leader of the government Mr. NORTHRUP.
had implicit confidence, or he would not have named Mr. Congdon as Governor of the Yukon-he would find the following :
2.	Will you agree to advocate for and insist upon the cancellation of the Treadgold concession ?
3.	Will you pledge yourself to advocate for and insist upon the punishment and exposure of officials. both in Dawson and Ottawa, by whose frauds or culpable negligence or inefficiency those concessions were granted In the first Instance or are now continued in force after the same by their terms should he cancelled ?
The answer given by Mr. Congdou to these questions is that Mr. Ross is out of the country, but ' I have no doubt he will advocate the course of action you suggest iu your questions.' We find that this was the state of affairs in the Yukon. Then this parliament meets. A representative is sent here from the Yukon; pledged to the lips to secure the cancellation of these infamous concessions and to have an investigation as to the fraud or culpable negligence or inefficiency of the officials either at Ottawa or Dawson, through whose fraud or negligence or inefficiency these concessions were granted. The; House met, and shortly afterwards a motion was brought up by my hon. friend from Montmorency ou this very subject; and the government, speaking by the mouth of the hon. Postmaster General, gave no uncertain sound. Those who were here when the hon. gentleman spoke, will remember well liow broadly be promised an investigation into these matters. The government was committed, if it is possible to commit a government by the solemn statements of one of its prominent members standing on the floor of parliament-and it is hard to conceive of any way in which a government can be committed if not in that way-to what ? Tq the following :
I would also say to my hon. friend who tella us that he is so desirous of investigation that I am sure he must well know that it has been long the fixed intention of the government to hold such an investigation.
We are told by the hon. Postmaster General that promises were made to the people of the Yukon that an investigation would be held into the whole administration of that territory, and now we can see why a representative was sent from the Yukon to support the government. The hon. Postmaster General said further :
I doubt if navigation is more than open, even if it is yet open. When the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Ross) returns to Ottawa,-he is at present in British Columbia, I understand- and we can have the benefit of his advice, it is our intention to fully carry out the representations made to the citizens of the Yukon to have a full investigation into all charges or suspicions that hon. gentlemen may be good enough to mention or entertain In regard to any matters connected with the Yukon administration. I give that public notice to my hon. friend, so that, in addition to the advantage he

has had of ventilating, his views on the floor of this House, he will have an opportunity to make good, if he can, any of his charges or suspicions before a tribunal where newspaper extracts and letters will not be the only evidence.	.
I do not think that any language could more clearly express the promise that we would be given a full investigation, not into the hydraulic needs of the Yukon, but into the charges and suspicions of fraud and corruption. Yet, to-night we have the sad spectacle of that same minister of the Crown, who made that pledge, standing up before this House-not denying that he used the language I have just quoted- but professing that the pledge then given is being carried out by the appointment of the Crown made the other day. Mr. Speaker, we may well pause to consider whose was the cowardly course, and whose honour is standing in the balance. With the words of the Postmaster General fresh in our recollection, let us consider what the authority of this commission really is, what ground it covers. There is a number of recitals :
That it has also been represented to the government that the extent and value of the deposits of gold in the benches, creeks and elevated ground is at present unknown and must remain so until a sufficient supply of water is available by the construction of hydraulic works, and that parties advancing moneys for the construction of said works must necessarily take great risks with respect to their Investments.
That is practical. That certainly relates to hydraulic operation.
That while it is fitting that such reasonable and proper privileges and advantages should be offered as will induce parties to construct such hydraulic works, yet it is essential that no grants or concessions should be made which will interfere with the right of water which any free miner is entitled to under the regulations governing placer mining In the Yukon Territory.
That the water so to be held and controlled by the hydraulic companies should be available on equal terms to all free miners whose claims can be profitably worked thereby.
That to obtain such hydraulic works and a supply of water for the benches, banks and elevated grounds above mentioned, certain powers, rights and privileges were grantel by the Governor General in Council on the 2lst of April, 1902 to Malcolm E. Orr-Ewing, A. N. C. Treadgold and Walter Barwick ; that it has been alleged

Alleged what ? Now we are coming to the sting of the whole inquiry.
That it has been alleged that the said grant and concession constitutes a monopoly, which, while depriving the treasury of an enormous revenue, is most detrimental to the mining industry of the Yukon.
It is perfectly true that that has been 1 alleged. No one on this side will deny it. But will any one pretend to say that that is ail that has been alleged ?
That it is important in the public interest that inquiry be made

We all agree with that, and we felt, with the words of the Postmaster General ringing in our ears, that at last justice was to be done, and that not only the charges but the mere suspicions were to be investigated.
for the purpose of obtaining information, showing to what extent the said grant and concession is likely to be beneficial or injurious to the mining interest of the said Yukon Territory.
That it is also desirable at the same time that the inquiry should not he limited to the said grant and concession

There we thought we were going to have something. We were going to get something at last. The hon. gentleman had repented, and even at the last moment they were going to give us what the Postmaster General promised solemnly, on the faith and honour of the government, we should have.
Showing to what extent the said grant is likely to be beneficial or injurious to the mining interests of the said Yukon Territory.
Then we read on. Another gleam of hope flashes across our mind, when we see that something more is to be investigated.
That it is further desirable that the commissioners making the inquiry shall investigate generally all the facts and circumstances

Here we felt certain we had it.
-which would afford information to parliament, to the government and to parliament

But our hearts sink within us as we go on to read :
-respecting the hydraulic or other mean3 which it is desirable should be adopted.
Is this what the House wants investigated, or what the people of the Yukon desire to have investigated ? It is not the hydraulic or other means hut the means whereby the government were deceived and misled that this House and the country want to see investigated. But when we are given this commission and are coolly told by the hon. Postmaster General that everything asked by the hon. member for Montmorency has been given, I ask again whose course is it that is cowardly, whose honour is at stake ? And I turn to the motion of my hon. friend from Montmorency for an answer. What do I find in that motion ? Among many clauses, I find this one :
That all hydraulic concessions whose owners have not observed the conditions of their leases and the provisions of the mining regulations may be rescinded.
That an inquiry may be set on foot to ascertain the circumstances under which the leading hydraulic concessions were obtained in order that action may be taken by the At or-ney General In the premises.
With that on the records of this House, moved by my hon. friend from Montmorency, the hon. the Postmaster General dared

to stand up and say that this Order in Council gives all-and he went beyond that, he out-heroded Herod, gives all and more than the hon. member for Montmorency asked.
Do I understand my hon. friend to say that he is reading from the motion of the hon. member for Montmorency ?
Yes.
No, you are reading from his speech.
I am not going to be diverted from the point by the hon. gentleman.

It is a question of fact. Is it the motion or the speech you are reading from ?
Mr., CASGRAIN. That is a paragraph of a resolution of the Liberal Club at Dawson. It is your own friends who said that.

I see that the hon. Minister of Justice is quite correct. In reading hurriedly a number of quotations marked here, I inadvertently read from the petition of the Liberal Club. The clause I read is in the petition of the Liberal Club of Dawson.
The hon. gentleman said it was in the motion.

My hon. friend from Montmorency used that petition of the Liberal Club along with other material that came from Dawson, to show that charges had been made into which he desired an investigation. When the governments' own friends make these charges, when one of their own supporters was sent to this House to have them investigated, and the ministers of the Crown promised that they should be investigated, we on this side expected more than was given. When we asked for bread, we did not expect such a stone as that. Hon. gentlemen opposite are very fond of taunting hon. members on this side with their obligation to make charges on their own responsibility, as members. It is very easy to make such a taunt, but it would be interesting to find how many members there are, either to your right or your left, Mr. Speaker, who know what the responsibility is that is incurred by a member so acting. I venture to say that outside the right hon. the first minister, there is not a member of this House who would declare that he knows what that responsibility is. I find on page 1040, of the ' Hansard ' of 1892, a speech made by the late Sir John Thompson, at the time when the famous Parent charges were made. He expressed himself to this effect, and there is no one in this House who will not admit that few brighter, abler and more prudent jurists ever sat in this House. And Sir John Thompson said :

1 am aware that there is a popular impression that a gentleman in this House who makes accusations of misconduct, impropriety, dishonesty. or other charges of that character against another member of this House incurs a serious responsibility, and may, if the charge is proven and unsustained be expelled from this Chamber. In view of the ground which I shall ask the House to take with regard to this resolution. I beg to call the attention cf hon. gentlemen to the fact, that that is an entire misapprehension. A member making a charge against another in this House may, of course, subject himself, as he does in pursuing pny line of conduct on any piece of business before the House, to the censure of the House ; but, so far as his own seat is concerned he may make false charges against other members of the House with perfect impunity.
It is perfectly true that, in the same debate, the present Premier (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) a few pages later, expressed himself to the contrary effect. He said :
The House expects from a member who makes a charge against a fellow member that he must have some good and strong reason for making that charge, and it is unquestionable that the common sense of the country would expect that, if any member should be guilty of making such foul charge against another member. without having strong reasons for making it and good evidence to support it, he would not be fit to associate with gentlemen and he ought to be expelled from this House.
So, on this point which has been so often referred to by lion, gentlemen opposite, surely, the ordinary member of this House may feel justified in being in some doubt when be finds that on so important a question as the Caron charges the Minister of Justice of that day and the leader of the present government, both gentlemen competent to speak, either of whose opinions, I am sure, any member of the House will bow to with the readiest deference, if they did not conflict-they are in such helpless conflict. But is that a fair taunt to throw at an hon. member on this side, when hon. members opposite are supposed to be equally interested with us in protecting the public property ? We find the charge made that the ministry has been imposed upon- and I wish to accentuate that, because it seems to lie assumed that the charge is in effect that Mr. This or Mr. That fraudulently and feloniously betrayed his trust. If such a charge were made it might fairly be said: There must be some responsibility behind it and if you were going to make a charge which would involve the political ruin of a member of this House, you must take some risk yourself. The charges made in the Yukon we wish to have investigated and the charges made in the Yukon are that that country has been robbed and ruined and an imposition practiced on the government. The whole question for this House to decide is whether we shall assume as a matter of fact and law that the government is so immaculate that it cannot be imposed upon, and therefore there should be no investigation. If we cannot come to that

conclusion, I say with all respect and regret, there is only one other conclusion possible, and that is that the hon. gentleman who glibly promised this investigation a few nights ago, as the people of this country will infallibly say, must have received further information since, which compels him now to retract what he said the other night, and not only, if I might use the expression, eat his own words, but insult the intelligence of this House by saying that this present Order in Council gives a wider investigation than we on this side either asked for or desire. Now, I do not intend to occupy the time of the House longer, for it seems to me as I said in the beginning, that the whole question can be boiled down into a very small compass. If we, sitting in this House are not to be at liberty to investigate charges of fraud on the government, charges made by the practically unanimous voice of the people of a large and important part of this country, men may well say under what condition may we ask to investigate such charges. And when we find in this debate, one minister promising full investigation and another saying that only the hydraulic powers and rights are to be investigated, and when we find ministers coming down, and, amid the clamour of their supporters, who evidently have not read the resolution, saying to this House in triumph, that they had given more than we had asked for, are we not justified in coming to the conclusion that hon. gentlemen opposite are inclined to use the pious editor's words and say :
In short, I firmly flu believe In humbug generally,
Fer it's a thing thet I perceive To hev a solid vally ;
This heth my faithful shepherd ben,
In pastures sweet heth led me,
An' this'll keep the people green To feed ez they hev fed me.

The difference between tweedledum and tweedledee is illustrated by the speakers here to-night. My hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Cas-grain) supported by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), charged that fraud has been practiced by the government. My hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) changed the charge and now rings the changes on the suggestion that fraud has been practiced on the government. Which of the two are we to deal with ? I do not know that I should have been called upon to interfere in this debate were it not that I think it to be my duty to defend my hon. friend from Montmorency to some extent against a charge that was not made but was possibly suggested by the_ lion. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock). The Postmaster General suggested. not that the hon. member for Montmorency was guilty of cowardice, but that, under the circumstances it looked like
cowardice, to take the position he did. I have known my hon. friend from Montmorency for many years. I knew him under circumstances where men soon learn to understand one another's characters especially with regard to matters of cowardice and bravery-I knew him at college. No man who ever had any knowledge of my hon. friend would charge him with being a coward, either a moral or a physical coward. He is neither one nor the other. But he is something else-he is a pastmaster in the art of obscuring an issue. We have had experience of one another for many years in the college and in the forum, and if any man knows well how to make much ado about nothing, my hon. friend does. Now, let us see what has taken place. Let me justify my charge that my hon. friend has proven, in connection with this debate, that he is a pastmaster in the art of obscuring an issue. He came here the other day and made a speech.
I need not say that it was an eloquent speech, for he scarcely ever speaks otherwise than eloquently. But after having gone through the speech, after having delivered himself of this oration and quoted copiously from resolutions passed by miners' conventions in the Yukon and so on, he finally offered a motion for the consideration of the House. I do not wish to weary the House with quotations, but I venture to make the statement that the pith of the whole motion is in these words :
This House is of opinion that the said powers, franchises and concessions constitute in favour of the said Treadgold and his associates a gigantic monopoly, which, while depriving the treasury of enormous revenues, is most detrimental to the mining industry of the Yukon.
That is the charge-that this concession constituted a monopoly and that the monopoly so constituted was most detrimental to the mining interests of the Yukon. What was there, then, to investigate ? That this was a monopoly went without saying-everybody admitted it. The thing was in its nature a monopoly, and we never pretended anything to the contrary. But what remained to be investigated was whether it was detrimental to the mining industry in the Yukon. What did we do ? Immediately when that motion was introduced a pledge was given that the charge made by my hon. friend would be investigated. What was the charge ? That this concession was detrimental to the interest of the Yukon. What do we find in the report to council upon which the commission issued ? The very words used by my hon. friend. This commission is appointed for the purpose of investigating that which he says was the result of the grant of this concession, that is to say, it was a concession detrimental to the interest of the Yukon. We use his own words in the order authorizing the investigation. Now, what

does he complain of ? Evidently my hon. friend knows when he produces an effect, because ordinarily he does produce an effect-but in another sphere when he is in court. He discovered that in this instance he failed entirely to produce any effect, either in this House or on public opinion, and he was forced to go to the newspapers immediately after and write a long and interesting letter, which had some effect, because it was in some respects interesting. But he was not satisfied with that, he found it necessary to do more. Finding the letter was not sufficient, he had to come here and make this motion to-night. Now, what do we find in his motion at the present time ? It is to the effect that the board of trade of the Yukon passed a resolution in which they said that this concession ' involved an enormous exploitation of the public resources of this territory for the benefit of a few favoured concessionaires.' Then he said :
That the Liberal Association of the city of Dawson, at a meeting held on the 1st of April, 1903. publicly denounced the said concessions as having been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation. and petitioned the government to institute an inquiry to ascertain the circumstances under which the leading hydraulic concessions were obtained in order that action may be taken by the Attorney General of Canada in the premises.
Then he goes on to say :
And this House is of the opinion that a special committee of this House should be appointed with all necessary powers to make a full and complete investigation, not only into the providence or improvidence of the terms and conditions of the several hereinbefore mentioned concessions, but also into all the circumstances relating to or connected with the granting or procurement of the same and all alterations therein, all negotiations and transactions between the government or any member or officer thereof and the said concessionaires or any person on their behalf with respect thereto or with respect to any alteration therein, the names of the persons directly or indirectly interested from time to time in the said concessions, the nature of their respective interests and the circumstances under which such interests were acquired.
What has that got to do with any charge
against the government ? What has that got to do with any suggestion of fraud by the government ? Is there a suggestion that there was fraud l>y the government ? Is there anything in this motion which would give the House to understand that my hon. friend is of opinion that fraud was practiced by the government, or by any member of the government, in connection with the granting of this concession ? No, he is a too honourable a man to make a statement which he knows is not true. But what does my hon. friend say ? He says the board of trade of the Yukon states that fraud was practiced on the government; he says that the Liberal Association of the Yukon echoes that charge. I have read Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
the petition sent here by the board of trade, and I cannot find anything to support my friend's assertion in it, that fraud was practiced on the government. But I will say this to my hon. friend, and here I know I will not appeal to him in vain. This concession was granted under the terms of the Dominion Lands Act, all these concessions were granted under the terms of that Act. Now there is no man in this House who knows better than my hon. friend that there is a door wide open, not only to the board of trade of the Yukon, not only to the members of the Liberal club, but to any man in the Yukon Territory or out of it, who honestly believes that fraud was practiced on the government iu connection with the granting of these concessions. The door is wide open ; Section 57 of the Dominion Lands Act, 49 Victoria, chapter 54 says :
Whenever patents, leases or other instruments, respecting lands have issued through fraud

That is the charge.
-or in error or improvidence, any court having competent jurisdiction in cases respecting real property in the province or territory where such lands are situate, may, upon action, bill or plaint respecting such lands, and upon hearing the parties interested, or upon default of the said parties after such notice of proceeding as the said court orders, decree or adjudge such patent, lease or other instrument to be void.
If fraud is practiced on the government there is a remedy, and ordinary fair play requires that that remedy should be applied, because every man who takes a patent from the Crown under the terms of the Dominion Lands Act takes it subject to all the conditions contained in that Act, and furthermore, takes it with the knowledge that the guarantees provided by that Act will surround the concession. He knows that if he has practiced fraud on the government he is exposed to have his interests brought before the Attorney General, and the Attorney General may issue a fiat for the purpose of testing the facts to ascertain whether fraud was practiced.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: Must it not be an individual who is interested in the fraud ? Can any person that is not interested bring a case ?

Any person having an interest, however remote, in the district affected, can act as a relator in applying to the Attorney General for his fiat for scire facias. I say that with all deference to the legal opinion of my bon. friend. Now, I say the courts are wide open to these gentlemen in the Yukon, and therein lies the secret of the motion that has been made here by my hon. friend. He knows full well that this remedy is afforded to these gentlemen ; he knows full well that if these men believe the charges they are making are well founded, there is a remedy open to them ; and knowing that,

knowing that they did not take advantage of the remedy that was open to them, he would not take the responsibility of adopting their charges and make them his own in this House ; he would not do it, because he knew full well that if they w7ere honest in their charges, if they could substantiate their charges, they might have done it elsewhere, and as they did not do it elsewhere, he would not take the responsibility of doing it for them.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have something in support of that. In the motion itself of my hon. friend we find that the Liberal Association of the city of Dawson, at their meeting held on the 1st of April last, were careful to indicate what they wanted to have done. They asked that an inquiry should be held to ascertain the circumstances under which the leading hydraulic concessions were obtained in order that action might be taken by the Attorney General in the premises. Why did they not apply for a scire facias ? Why did they not adopt the remedy which the law gives them ? They were on the ground, they were cognizant of the facts. They had all the material at their disposal ; why did they not petition the Attorney General for a fiat ? I make the statement here and now, in the hearing of the Prime Minister, and with the authority of the government, that if an application of that sort is made it won't take five minutes to grant it, and an opportunity will be given to these gentlemen to make good their charges. More than that. In these instructions to the commission, what do we find ? We find they have gone very far in the direction of meeting this request of the gentlemen connected with the Liberal club of the Yukon. They say an inquiry should be made for the purpose of ascertaining the circumstances under which the hydraulic concessions were obtained in order that action may be taken by the government. The commissioner is required to investigate, not only the circumstances connected with the concession to Treadgold, but the instruction provides also :
That it is also desirable at the same time that the inquiry should not he limited to the said grants and concession but should extend to all similar hydraulic concessions granted in the Yukon Territory.
For what purpose ?
The inquiry is to be general. The inquiry is to be held into all the circumstances connected with these different concessions.
No, no.

Will my hon. friend pardon me ?
5lr. CASGRAIN. It is not correct.

I accept the correction of my hon. friend. The inquiry is to be held for the purpose of ascertaining the facts and circumstances connected with all these concessions. The facts and circumstances will necessarily imply an investigation into the circumstances of these concessions which were granted. If it appears that fraud was practiced, the information will be in the possession of the government, but in the meantime it is open for any one to proceed as provided in the Dominion Lands Act. Let any responsible man come forward and make such charges as will justify the issue of a fiat and he will not have long to wait for it. I shall be content with recapitulating what has taken place. My hon. friend made his charge on the 12th May in regard to the Treadgold matter. He said it. ought to be investigated. We granted an investigation. He is not satisfied with that investigation, but he says that we ought to inquire into all the facts and circumstances connected with that matter for the purpose of ascertaining whether a fraud was practiced on the government or on the public. The remedy is open to him under the Dominion Lands.Act. I was not here when he began his speech, but I understand that my hon. friend found fault with the government for having chosen a judge to act in this matter. Hon. gentlemen opposite have reiterated the statement during the course of this debate that this was not a political matter, that all that was desired by them was to have an honest investigation into all the facts and circumstances connected with this concession, so that we might know whether or not it was providently or improvidently issued or whether this concession was tainted with fraud. They say it is not proper to assign a judge to perform the duties which are to be imposed upon Mr. Justice Britton and the commissioners to be appointed hereafter. My hon. friend did me the honour of quoting me in connection with the use of the judicial office for such inquiries. Would he allow me to reciprocate ? My hon. friend was attorney general in ttfie province of Quebec and occupied in respect to that province the position which I occupy in respect to the Dominion of Canada. In 1902 charges were made involving political dishonesty on the part of political men- very serious charges of the grossest political dishonesty. My hon. friend did not hesitate to appoint a judge to make the investigation. He appointed three of them. He appointed one of them who was fresh from the fray, having been only recently appointed to the bench. I do not say that he acted improperly at that time. Far be it from me to contend anything of the sort.
May I ask the hon. gentleman who that was ?
It was Mr. Justice Baby.
He was not fresh from the fray. He had been on the bench for fifteen or twenty years.
He had been sitting in this House a year or two before he was appointed.
No, ten years before.
At all events a short time before.
It was ten years .before.
I say two years before, and my hou. friend says ten years before. The Prime Minister suggests that we are both wrong and fixes the time at five years. I believe it is five. In medio stat veritas.
The bon. gentleman must know that I had nothing to do with appointing Mr. Justice Baby, because I was not attorney general at the time.

I think that is correct. My hon. friend was not attorney general at the very moment, but he became attorney general a short time after, and, I presume, assumed responsibility for that act. Does my hon. friend remember another commission appointed in Montreal, I think, by him ?
Yes.
That one was a judge.
Yes.
And appointed by my hon. friend.
And that is one of the reasons why I believe after past experience that these appointments to royal commissions are not a success.

If my hon. friend will pardon me then he will have to leave it to me to say in future what my past experience has been. I contend that it would be desirable that our judges should be as far removed from politics as possible. I have had twenty years' experience at the bar and I have been engaged in a very great number of cases, sometimes for the Tories and sometimes for the Liberals. I have have been a little bit on both sides-not politically-but at the bar. and in all my experience I have never felt that I could appeal to the past and say that any judge had acted improperly from a political standpoint in any case I had before him. The experience which I have had has been such as to justify me in the belief that the judges of our country have been far removed from politics and that they are always prepared to do their duty.
Tory judges.

My hon. friend (Mr. Rosamond) should not try to distinguish because there are those who think you should not judge others by the knowledge you have of your own. Under the circumstances, what has been done ?

Mr. Justice Britton has been selected. This after all is an inquiry into an hydraulic concession, into what is after all nothing more nor less than ditches on a large scale. That is the explanation of the Treadgold matter. It is nothing more nor less than an inquiry into the conditions and circumstances under which water is distributed in the Yukon Territory. Mr. Justice Britton had a large experience in connection with matters of this sort in the province of Ontario as drainage commissioner. In addition to that there is an hydraulic engineer whose name has been mentioned in connection with the commission. Whether or not we can secure the services of this gentleman, I do not know, but to show the intention of the government an hydraulic engineer of continental reputation, against whose character not one breath of suspicion can be cast, was selected merely because of the professional position which he occupied. We have taken all the precautions to give my hon. friend what he wanted when he first moved in this matter, but it appears that be is satisfied, not that he did not go far enough in the first instance with the material he had, because no fresh material has been produced before the House, but that he did not go far enough to satisfy those who are desirous of lending a willing ear to street gossip and rumours, and to those who appear anxious to slander their neighbours to death, but have not got courage to come out as a man should, if a reflection has been put on any man, to charge that man and say he is guilty of wrongdoing, feeling satisfied that there is enough independence in this House to say whether he be guilty or not.
Will tbat commission sit in Ottawa ?	*

This commission will naturally sit in the Yukon Territory to inquire into the facts submitted to it and especially for the purpose of inquiring into the fact as to whether these concessions were necessary and as to whether under the circumstances existing there, this hydraulic concession was a provident or an improvident one. But after having caused an inquiry on the ground, their duty would be to come here and hold any investigation that would be necessary under the circumstances. I think that having said that, I have shown the good faith of the government-of course they are not limited as to time, place and circumstance- and the desire of the government to have a thorough and honest investigation to establish two things. First, was the concession issued improvidently; was it contrary to the interest of the Yukon that such a concession should be granted; and second, was such fraud practiced on the government as would justify the government in coming to the conclusion-not to repeal the concession; there is no authority to repeal a concession for fraud; there is no author-
I

ity to repeal a concession for misrepresentation-but there is authority to take proceedings before the court for the purpose of having the concession set aside.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

Before this debate comes to a conclusion I deem it my duty to refer to an incident which has taken place in connection with it, and which I think ought not to pass unnoticed. Twice within a few days any hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has made the insinuation on the floor of this House, that I had been approached by some one who had made charges to me that there had been wrongdoing in this concession. Some few days ago my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) stated that while I was in London last summer some one had made similar charges to me. I denied the statement at the titue. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) repeated it to-day in a more aggravated form and with greater emphasis. I gave it the denial which I should give it, and now for the third time I have to say to my hon. friend that there is not the slightest foundation for the insinuation he has made.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Does the right hon. gentleman say that I made an insinuation ?
Yes, Sir.
I asked if there was any truth in what had been said, and I made no insinuation at all myself.
My hon. friend put the question to me the other day and I denied it, and when on a subsequent occasion he reasserts it I take that to be an insinuation.
I made no assertion. I deny that, Mr. Speaker. I asked if there was any truth in these remarks. I will not allow even the right hon. gentleman to put words in my mouth which I did not utter.
I am speaking within the knowledege of the House-
My words are in * Hansard.'

' Hansard ' is my best authority, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) stated the other day that I had been approached by some one in England and that similar circumstances had been brought to my notice. I then denied it. To-day the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) within the hearing of everybody on the floor of the House again put a question to me and after my denial, if that is not an insinuation I do not know what is.
Hear, hear.

When I stated here as a member of parliament, and I believe as a man of honour; at all events
with the responsibilities I hold, that there was no such thing as had been stated the other day, and when the hon. gentleman again repeats it, for my part I take it to be an insinuation. If it is not an insinuation it is certainly not an accusation, and if it is not an insinuation or an accusation then I leave it to my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) to say what he thinks of it.

Since my right hon. friend asks me; what I stated the other day was this :	That these things were being said
in the city of Montreal that when my right hon. friend was there the matter had been brought to his notice, and what I stated to-day was that it has been circulated also in the city of Montreal that upon the return of my right hon. friend the matter had been brought to his notice by the chief of the executive. I made no insinuation.

Well, I shall not parry the point any longer. I must however say to my hon. friend that the fact of his having twice asked me on the floor of the House whether or not I had been approached by some body with that charge of wrong-doing about this concession, implies that some one has gone to my hon. friend; that some one has poured something in his; ear, that some one has gone to my hon. friend and stated to him; that either that man himself or some one else had come to me with charges of wrong-doing in connection with that concession. Now, the man who went to my hon. friend whoever he is and who stated to him that I had been approached either by himself or by some one else, that man must have a name; he must have a reputation; he must have a character since the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) thinks it worth while to put questions to me about it. If he has no name; if he has no character; if he has no reputation, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) was very wrong to make this statement of a worthless man the basis of a question to me.
Hear, hear.

But if lie had a name, if he had a reputation, if he had a character and if he made the statement, why has not the hon. gentleman the courage to repeat that statement by taking the responsibility for it on the floor of this House. It is his duty. He has information or he has not. The information that he has is worth something or it is worth nothing, and since the hon. gentleman has found it worth his while to put these questions to me in my official position. I assume the hon. gentleman attaches some responsibility to his information whoever his informant may be. If his informant has told him anything, and if his informant is worth anything, why in the name of common sense, why in the name of fair-play, why in the name of honour between man

and man, between members of parliament; wliy does be not come out with the charge that has been made to him. If any one has told him a tale whether it is true or false; if any one has told him a tale which he believes to be true, he knows his duty and his right as a member of parliament. Two or three years ago my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) had a tale poured in his ears in connection with the South African war affecting the honour or supposed to affect the honour of a trusted colleague of mine, the Minister of Militia. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) did not hesitate then to come forward with his charge; he thought he had proof behind him. But to-day neither my bon. friend or anybody else will tiike the responsibility of stating what are these charges of fraud and misrepresentation. The atmosphere is thick to-day with the words fraud and misrepresentation. The word ' fraud ' is very vague; fraud may take a multitude of forms; misrepresentation may be of different characters and I ask my hon. friend, I will ask anybody in this House-I will not even appeal to my own friends-but I will ask anybody on that side of the House in the name of fair-play and justice, what are we to investigate when we do not even know the name of a witness. If fraud has been perpetrated who has committed the fraud; wliat is the character of the fraud ? If misrepresentation has been committed to the minister or to anybody else, wliat is the character of the misrepresentation ? If there is somebody to tell us that this fraud is so and so and such and such, that there has been such an act perpetrated by which the government has been imposed upon, then .we would know where to go for evidence and for the facts which are going to be investigated, but shall it be said in an assembly of serious men, in an assembly of men such as we are here: that wie shall cause investigation to go simply upon the use of the two words ' fraud and misrepresentation ? ' Who are to be the witnesses, and if we are to appoint commissioners to investigate these frauds and misrepresentations, surely we would have to give them the names of the witnesses and the facts which would have to be investigated ? Sir, I have only to say upon this occasion that if the charges are formulated in the proper manner they shall be investigated. My hon. friend who leads the opposition appealed to me to act as we did in the Drummond County Railway charges. There was a great difference between the Drummond County Railway charges and the charges made upon this occasion. When the Drummond County Railway charges were investigated there had been made by a pro? niinent member of parliament, direct accusations against one of my colleagues. It was important that these should be investigated. Although we granted an investigation at that time, it turned out after all

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
that those charges were absolutely futile.
It turned out that when the parties who made the charges were brought face to face with the investigation, they said they7 had nothing to prefer. Under such circumstances, I do not think that is a precedent to follow; but the precedent to follow is the rule that if a man is accused, fie has a right to know who are his accusers, and what is the accusation against him.

Mr. Speaker, as the right hon. gentleman has made some personal references to myself, I will quote from ' Hansard ' what I said the other day :
Everybody knows that, and I demur to the proposition of my right hon. friend that a man is obliged, when he hears these rumours current in the public, when time and place and circumstances are stated-when it is stated, for instance, that my right hon. friend, himself, when he was in England, was made aware of certain circumstances connected with this matter-
I deny that absolutely.
So much the better, Mr. Speaker; but I say that has been stated, and I demur to the proposition that we are here for the purpose of bringing accusations.
Do it, then. Do it, then.

We are here for the purpose of conveying to the House the sentiments of the public and what is stated in the public.
I did not go further than that, Mr. Speaker, and when this evening I alluded to the same affair, I said it had been uttered in Montreal and elsewhere that the attention of the Prime Minister had been called to this concession upon his return to this country, by His Excellency the Qovernor General, and I asked him if that was the case. Now, Sir, in spite of what has fallen from the lips of my right hon. friend, I deny that I can be deprived in this House, as a representative of the people, of the right of stating what is current on the street, and asking for information on these questions from hon. gentlemen who sit on the treasury * benches. I have made no charge. I have said this evening that I do not know where the wrong-doing took place ; but I claimed that we should have such an investigation as would enable all those who had taken part in that transaction to he heard before a committee of this House.

Mr. Speaker, before you put the question, I want to say a few words in regard to my friend the Hou. Mr. Ross, who is absent from the House. I do not think it is right for hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to place Mr. Ross in a false position in this matter. The hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup), who I am sorry is not in his seat at present, made the statement that Mr. Ross was pledged to the lips to have the Treadgold concession cancelled. Now, I want to say that Mr. Ross

did nothing of the kind. Mr. Ross subscribed to the platform of the Liberal party in the Yukon. In other words, he promised that an investigation would be held, and an investigation is going to be held. The hon. member for East Hastings also made reference to something Mr. Congdon had said. 1 do not think Mr. Ross is responsible for any statement that Mr. Congdon made in his absence. The government is carrying out any promise that Mr. Ross made to* the people of the Yukon at that time. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) insinuated that the hon.
