Minister of the Interior was in some manner connected with this transaction. He did not go so far as to mention the name of the Minister of the Interior, but he mentioned the department.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I said that it was in that department that these concessions were carried through, and I repeat it.

What is that but an insinuation ? If these hon. gentlemen have anything to say with reference to the Minister of the Interior, they are well aware that he will be in this House in eight or ten days. They will then have an ample opportunity, if they have any charges to make against him, to make those charges on their responsibility as members of this House. It would be well for them to remember that an hon. gentleman in the last parliament, whom some of them are imitating to-night, spoke for nine hours in reciting charge after charge, which he refused to take the responsibility of making ; and what was the consequence ? The leader of the opposition at that time, Sir Charles Tupper, repeated the charges which had been made by the hon. member for Pictou (Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper). The leader of the opposition of that day and the hon. member for Pictou, who is absent from the House, had a great deal more courage than some of these hon. gentlemen have to-night. They had the courage to go outside and make on the public platform the charges which they had made in this House; and what was the consequence ? The leader of the opposition made the charge all over the country, that the Minister of the Interior had been connected with his law partner at Brandon in granting some licenses for the sale of liquor in the Yukon ; but when Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper spoke at a meeting in Brandon during the election of 1900 repeating those charges he was met with a letter written by Sir Charles Tupper, sr., in which he had taken everything back. I can read the letter if hon. gentlemen would like to hear it, as it is very interesting reading. This is the letter as it appears in the Winnipeg ' Free Press : '
Dear Sir,-Referring to a speech made by me at Brandon on the_ 20th of November last, during 'which you claim I made certain damaging references to you in reference to the importation or alleged importation of liquor into the Yukon Territory, I beg to say that such speech was intended to be directed by me entirely to a discussion of public questions, and my intention was not to reflect in any way upon you personally. If any of those present took a different meaning from what I said I now beg to say that subsequent investigation has shown me that the telegram sent in your name to Mr. Sifton on the 12th of June, 1898, asking that the letter in question should be amended so as to include the importation of liquor into the Yukon, and which telegram was referred to by Mr. Sifton on the floor of the House of Commons as having been received by him from you, was not sent or authorized by you and that you did not directly or indirectly in any way through yourself or any other person take or attempt to take liquor into the Yukon Territory under the authority of the letter given by Mr. Sifton to which I referred in my remarks, and that you were no party directly or indirectly to the attempt made to dispose of the liquor. I further beg to state that I have satisfied myself that there is no ground for believing that yourself or Mr. Sifton were concerned together in taking or attempting to take liquor into the Yukon Territory. I sincerely regret if anything which I said has been construed into a reflection on your character.
That letter is signed by Sir Charles Tupper. It was sent only after a writ was issued. The leader of the opposition went through this country repeating those statements on platform after platform, and when he found that he was going to be dragged into court, he wrote this apology. After repeating this all through the country, we find that he had to take it all back. It is within the memory of every hon. gentleman who had a seat in the last parliament that statements were made in this House charging the hon. Minister of the Interior with I do not know what. I could read you a nine hours speech of Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper, making all sorts of Insinuations, and if the government are to be stampeded every time any hon. gentleman chooses to repeat gossip or make insinuations against them, we would have commissions appointed every day in the week. The hon. Minister of the Interior will be here in ten or twelve days, and if any hon. gentleman opposite has any charges to make, let him do as the exMinister of Public Works did some years ago, take the responsibility of making them and no doubt he will get ail the investigation he wants.

speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

speechtext: Has the hon. minister ever considered the advisability of establishing a model farm in the province of Quebec, which would be more easily acceptable than the experimental farm here ? I have several times brought this matter to his attention.

I believe that the money which would be required for such a farm could be used more effectively in other ways. When the farm at Ottawa was established, it was considered that it would serve the two provinces of Quebec and Ontario. The climate and conditions in Ottawa are similar to those of a great part of the province of Quebec and also Ontario, and I think that the experiments carried on here are as useful to the farmers of Quebec as they are to the farmers of Ontario.
Mr. DEMERS (St. John and Iberville.) (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, we should not lose sight of the fact that the province of Quebec is essentially agricultural. The maritime provinces could dispense with an experimental farm more easily than we could. I have ascertained by myself that the Ottawa farm is useful to our farmers. A great number of those who do not live very far from it are pleased to come and visit it every year ; but, as it will be admitted, that farm is of no easy access to the many. Therefore, I hope the government will have this matter under serious consideration, and that the province of Quebec will, before long, get that farm to which, in my opinion, it is rightly entitled.

If I remember well, the last time this question was brought up the hon. minister said he would give the question consideration. I do not know whether a register is kept of the farmers from the province of Quebec who visit the experimental farm, but there is no doubt whatever that a model farm, one that would not cost anything as excessive as the institution here, centrally situated in the province of Quebec and easy of access, would be of immense benefit to the young farmers of the province. It seems to me that three or four years ago, when the minister said that the matter was engaging his attention. Has he given it any further thought ?

The matter has been brought to my attention several times and I have discussed it in all its bearings. The hon. gentleman speaks of a record of the number of farmers from Quebec that come to the farm. No record is kept in that form. The great bulk of the farmers come here in excursions organized from one locality or another. I feel safe in saying that more farmers come from the province of Quebec to visit the experimental farm than come from the province of Ontario, and I say that with pride, as being a representative of the province of Quebec. It shows an interest in progressive agriculture amongst the farmers of Quebec that is most creditable and satisfactory.
What becomes of the butter manufactured in the experimental farm ?
It is sold in Ottawa.
Is a record kept of the disposal that is made of it ?
Yes. I am informed that the question was asked in the House some time ago and was fully answered.

I do not think it was. I would be glad if, when the hon. minister's estimates are next before the committee, he would have his officials bring down the book containing the record of the sales of butter manufactured at the experimental farm. It cannot be a very voluminous document, and I should like to look at it.
I shall be glad to do so.

For some years one portion of the experimental farm, two hundred acres in extent, has been set apart to be conducted as a farmer would conduct his own business. I would like to know the result, allowing a fair estimate of interest on the investment and also the expenses of working. I think this would be the most valuable Information the experimental farm could give, because it would show the working of a farm in the ordinary way. We get great reports of the experiments in the 143J
small plots and we sometimes think that more attention is placed with the small plots than a regular farmer could give. Therefore, it would be very interesting to get a report upon this two-hundred-acre farm.

That suggestion was made last session, and it is being carried out. But the year has not yet closed. A day-book is kept on the farm with a record of the work of every labourer. Labour, of course, is changed about from that part of the farm to the experimental farm and the same way with the teams. When the current year is closed, the accounts will be made up.

I moved a resolution last year for a return of this kind. Either I did not make the resolution broad enough or the answers were incomplete. I did not get the information I sought. If the hon. minister would promise to give us, at the end of the year, the report that I have suggested, I think it would be satisfactory to the people.

I do not remember the exact terms of the resolution, but I remember the terms of the discussion. I think the information called for was in the form in which the book-keeping had been done up to that time-that is, each crop and field was reckoned by Itself. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson) or some other hon. gentleman suggested the other method and that method is being worked out for the present year.

In the return brought down a team taken from the ordinary experimental part of the farm and used so many hours was only allowed for at a certain rate for the number of hours employed. The same way with labour. But you could not run an ordinary farm that way. If you wanted a team of horses you would have to keep them the year round, and if you wanted a man you could not employ him for a few hours and then let him go.
But when we charge by the hour in that way, we charge more than the actual cost of keeping the horses.
But, the hon. gentleman must admit that the system hardly works out the fair result in comparison with the ordinary farm.

I think it gives a result against the farm here at Ottawa. I know enough about the farm book-keeping to know that a team can be kept for the whole year at a moderate cost. The rate charged against the farm here, I believe, is S3 per day for man and team. If that rate were charged against the ordinary farm for the number of days' work done, the amount would more than cover the expense of keeping the man and team for the whole year.
And interest on the investment also ?
Interest oil the equipment is charged separately.

In the next report, will the minister give us a full account of the total cost of working the 200 acres ?
The S1INISTER OF AGRICULTURE. I think in the next annual report we will have a full statement of the expense of working that 200.acres as a whole.

The minister said a few moments ago that the number of visitors to the farm at Quebec was larger than from Ontario. Some persons might draw the inference that the farmers of Ontario were not as anxious for information as the farmers of Quebec. There are some facts to account for that. In the first place, the central farm at Ottawa is quite a long distance from the bulk of the farming population of Ontario, and they would require to be here over night. Probably most hon. gentlemen know that we have an excellent college farm at Guelph, to which pilgrimages are made during the summer by farmers' institutes all over the country. They can go and come back in a day ; therefore, they patronize that farm at Guelph rather than come to Ottawa. I have often thought that it was desirable that farmers' excursions should be arranged from some parts of central Ontario to visit the experimental farm. I know they already get the benefit of the reports that are distributed, but I think they would see something to their advantage if they observed the working of the farm.

Probably there are more individual farmers coming from Ontario than from Quebec; but the large excursions which visit the farm come more frequently from Quebec. What my hon. friend says with regard to the farm at Guelph is no doubt quite correct.
should take the whole 200 acres of land that is worked as a farm, and charge it with all the labour and work put upon it, and give it credit for all it produces. That is what we are trying to work out now, and which will appear in the next year's report. A record is now being kept of each crop or each series of crops. Hitherto we never took the whole of the 200 acres and treated it as an entity. We took each individual crop or field of grain- on that 200 acres, each individual cow or herd of cows, and dealt with them, charging everything that is spent upon them and crediting them with everything they produce. But in addition to that, I understood that the hon. gentleman asked last session that we should keep a book for the whole farm collectively, without reference to the individual fields and crops. We will still continue the old system of charging to the individual fields and crops, so that we will be able to work out what the hon. gentleman alludes to in the future as we have been doing in the past. To-day we know the profits of each crop of oats, of wheat, of roots, and of each cow in the dairy, and we will continue that system of accounts, because we think it is absolutely essential to good book-keeping. But in addition to that we are going to keep a separate account of the collective work of the 200 acres.

Last year some criticism was made of the fact that in the statement furnished to the House by way of a return, $3 a day was charged for a man and a team. But there was no undertaking on the part of the government to account for all the labour that was paid for out of the vote that was given by this House to carry on the farm generally. The hon. gentleman charges $3 a day for a certain service, for a man and a team, but he does not show the cost of the whole outfit. That service might require the use of a roller, or of a drill, or a plough and harrow. We would like to know', not only how much the whole farm has paid, but how much each branch has paid or lost.

The hon. gentleman ljas not told us what mode he follows of keeping the accounts. I understood him to say last year that at a later date the accounts would be presented at the end of the fiscal year which had been prepared in a different manner from the mode adopted hitherto.

It has been suggested that wTe adopt a new system of book-keeping. Under the present system each field is charged with the labour expended upon it, and credited with the returns obtained from it. For instance, w'e charge that field the number of day's *work, either of men or of horses. I understood the request last session was that instead of charging each crop, reckoning up against each crop what we put upon it, we
That is what we propose to try and do.
What stock has been purchased during the year past ?

1 have not got a list of all the animals. But we are constantly purchasing pigs, for instance, and selling them. During the last twelve months. I have directed that some French Canadian cattle should be purchased for the farm. Speaking from memory, we have not purchased any other thoroughbred animals except five head of French Canadian cattle, a bull and four cows. I think we purchased one or two grade animals, but we purchase and sell them according to the exigencies of the time, or according to what we require of
them. I am speaking without reference to the number of steers that we purchase every fall which we feed and sell again as beef.
Is it the intention to make this farm pay as a farm, or are the experiments that are there conducted regarded as a part of the revenue ?

I think that perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Ross, Ontario) may not remember that about three years ago I divided the farm, taking 200 acres of it and setting it apart as' a farm with a regular rotation of crops and without any reference to the experimental work. That was put in charge of the agriculturist, Mr. Grisdale. He was informed that lie must buy no manure and that he must keep as much stock as he could feed and see whether he could improve the fertility of that 200 acres, and show that it could be done at a profit. The whole farm includes 465 acres, and of this 200 is treated as a farm. The other 265 acres, including the orchard, arboretum, woodland, roads and buildings, as well as the land, are devoted especially to experimental work.

I look upon the 200 acres as the more valuable part of the experimental farm. I think that we ought to get information not only as to the crops that it pays best to raise, but as to the kind of stock that can be kept on a farm of a given number of acres, the number of cattle, pigs and sheep and the kind of implements the farmer requires. We should have all this information, because I think it is the most practical part of the experimental farm, and I think it would be of more interest to the farmers than anything else.
I quite agree with the hon. gentleman.

May I ask the hon. minister if he is making any special experiments at the farm, or is the same routine work carried on every year ? Perhaps the hon. gentleman could tell us of some line of work that was carried on during last year. There are consttmt improvements and changes going on in regard to the farming interest and we would naturally expect the experimental farm would be in advance of every other farm.

I could not off-hand give the hon. gentleman details of all the experiments that are being tried this year. There are certain classes of experiments which extend over a long term of years. Experiments have been carried on as to the fertilization and treatment of soils. There was an exhaustive series of experiments conducted in regard to the fertilization of land by growing clover crops, and it took eight or ten years to prove the results, although we saw the effect earlier. We required to take that time to be sure that the effect of this treatment will
be permanent. There are during every year experiments iu the different methods of treating soil and in the growing of grain crops. These experiments are going on every year and we are steadily accumulating an immense mass of information which is from time to time worked up by the officers of the farm into details of the results and these results are published in bulletins and in the annual report. I do not at the moment remember any new thing that has been started this season. I was out at the farm the other day and was shown by the agriculturist an experiment tided for the first time in regard to the width between the rows or drills in sowing grain. Instead of sowing the drills all the same width apart, we have alternated the spaces. In one instance one of the spouts of the seeder is stopped and in another the whole of the spouts are used. Last year we tried very considerable experiments in ridging up part of the field and leaving it ridged up during the winter to show the effect of frost and to ascertain what the result would be in the spring in drying off and preparing the soil for the crop. One piece of land was rigged up and another left in the ordinary way. We are trying things of that kind all the time and they are explained in detail by the officers of the farm who come before the Committee on Agriculture of the House. They also appear in the annual report every year.
How many teams of working horses, how many other horses and how many cattle have you on the farm ?

I could not off-hand say how many horses or cattle are on the farm. I have just asked the director and he cannot from memory state positively. There are between thirty-five and forty milk cows, about sixteen horses, four or five bulls and about two hundred pigs and about forty sheep. All these details are in the annual report which hon. members have.
Can the hon. gentleman tell the committee how many thoroughbreds there are on the farm and how many grades?
There are, I think, about twenty pure bred cows. Then, all the bulls are pure bred.
How many ?

There are five pure bred bulls, one Shorthorn, one Ayrshire, two Guernseys and one French Canadian. There are four French Canadian cows, six or seven Guernsey cows, eight or nine Ayrshire cows, and about five Shorthorn milking cows and some that are going to be milking very soon.
Has there been any pure bred stock bought during the present year ?
I bought five French Canadian animals.
Are they considered pure bred ?
Certainly. They are registered animals, and the purest blood there is on the continent of America.
I understand that you had some of that breed years ago ?
Yes ; ten or twelve years ago, but none remained.
What was the result with these French Canadian animals ?
The result was to show that the French Canadian cow is a very economical producer of butter, giving a rich milk and costing comparatively little to feed.
How do they compare with the other breeds ?
I cannot speak as to the result of the tests in detail. I cannot say positively whether the French Canadian cows ten years ago on the farm showed up better than the short horns or the Ayrshire*.
The minister must have had some reason to continue the experiment.

I am pretty familiar with the breed myself in the province of Quebec, and know how excellent they are. The general average of milk in the province of Quebec is extremely rich, and the French Canadian cow has played a very important part in rendering the butter production of that province so high. At the Buffalo exhibition, in a dairy test lasting six months, the French Canadian herd made so fine a showing as to attract attention from one end of the continent to the other, with the result that there are now large sales of French Canadian cattle to the United States, as well as to the other provinces of Canada.
Which breed would it be advisable for a farmer'to keep for general purposes ?
I would not presume to answer. It depends on the farmer's taste and the markets he has to supply.
We find Shorthorns and Ayrshires crossed to be about the best.
Some people do.
What has been the result of your experiments in regard to the causes of soft pork ?

The whole matter was fully published in a Hon. Mr. FISHER.
special bulletin which was issued two years ago.
We had the gentleman who prepared that bulletin before the Agricultural Committee, and his evidence was of the most unsatisfactory kind.
Whom do you refer to ?
I have forgotten his name, but he has been in the department long before the minister.
I suppose it was Mr. Shutt, who, with Mr. Grisdale, conducted the experiments.

An experiment was being made in one of the packing bouses in the city of Ottawa, and Mr. Shutt prepared a report, which was published broadcast from one end of this country to the other, of a most damaging character, if it was true. Mr. Shutt, when he appeared before the committee, was unable to verify the statements he had made in the report, and was compelled to admit that the reasons he had given why the pork was soft were mere conjectures. The bulletin contained the statement that a number of small pigs had been purchased in the corn district, and, without having any evidence as to their having been fed on a single grain of corn-in fact, they were of the age when they could not be fed on grain of that kind-he came to the conclusion that because they had come from what was alleged to be the corn district, that was the reason their pork was soft. It seems to me that a statement of that kind ought not to be made in the country, because it would convey the impression that all the pork brought from the west would be soft. I would like to ask the minister if these experiments have been since continued, or if he considers the case closed on the report of Mr. Shutt ?

I must say that I am very much surprised at what the hon. gentleman says. The report speaks for itself. The officers who worked out the experiment consider that the report settled the matter, as far as an experiment of that kind could settle it. What the hon. gentleman says as to some of the hogs having been bought in what he calls the corn belt is perfectly true ; but that does not imply that they were fed on corn. The question was whether pigs which had been fed very largely on corn for a generation or two were practically born with a predisposition to make soft pork instead of hard pork ; and to test that question we bought some of the pigs we were experimenting with from the corn belt. Borne of these pigs were fed on one thing and *6me on another, and the results were worked out in the report. I cannot repeat the conclusions exactly, but the hon. gentleman knows them as well as I do.

I can inform the hon. gentleman that there was no such conclusion drawn from the report as that from the long feeding of pigs on corn in the corn belt they had an inherent tendency to make pork that must necessarily be soft.

I did not say that any such conclusion was drawn. I said that we bought the pigs for the purpose of ascertaining what the results were. The results are shown in the report: I cannot tell the hon. gentleman what those results were.

The hon. gentleman knows what that report contains. The hon. gentleman knows that it is a pure assumption that because these pigs came from the west that must be the reason the pork was soft. There is no evidence to support that assumption. There is nothing to show that on the farm from which they were taken they were not fed on mixed food. It was boldly assumed that by reason of their coming from that locality, the pork would necessarily be soft. Attention was called to this in the committee, and Mr. Shutt was compelled to admit that this was merely a conclusion of his own. I do not think the case should rest there. I think the matter is of such importance in the west, where large quantities of pork are being produced, that it should not be put under the ban of such a shadow of suspicion as that. I do not think it is fair to that part of the country, and I would like to know whether the hon. minister is now prosecuting the matter, or whether he intends to leave it in the shape in which it was, I think unfairly, left in the report.
My answer is that the report speaks for itself. I am not going to dispute with the hon. gentleman as to quotations from the report, as I do not remember it sufficiently to quote from it.

I do not think that is a proper answer to the hon. member for Both-well. As he contends that the report was altogether in error and misleading, and against the interests of western Ontario, particularly that part of the country in which corn is grown, he wants to know whether the minister is going to prosecute this inquiry further, to see whether or not his officers are mistaken. If he is not, he can tell the hon. member so ; but if he is determined to prosecute the inquiry further, it would be very interesting to members from the west to know that their interests are still being looked after by the Minister of Agriculture.
What I say is that I cannot quote the report, but my memory of it is that it contains no such reflections on the corn-belt pigs as the hon. gentleman supposes.

We do not expect the hon. minister to remember the report. He pays so little attention to his department, being sometimes in England, sometimes in France, and sometimes in Japan, with a deputy minister who perhaps does not know the difference between hard pork and soft pork, and with a chemist who perhaps even does not eat bacon, but requires something a little more fanciful, we do not expect that the minister is going to be able to keep in mind these particular things which interest the farmers so much. We want to know, whether the hon. gentleman is going to send broadcast throughout this country reports of a flimsy character, which are misleading and calculated to do a great deal of injury to the agricultural community ? We want to know whether he is going to spend some of this money in making further investigations with a view of having the matter entirely before the country ?

The report is not a flimsy one but the result of two years investigation by the most competent officers in the department. Professor Shutt is a man whose standing no one would dare dispute, Professor Saunders is the man who organized the whole farm and worked it up from the beginning. It ill-beeomes the hon. gentleman to east unfair reflections on these officers. I am only the political head and do not take credit for this work, but to say that it is a flimsy affair is a statement which, to any one who knows the two gentlemen in question, refutes itself.
There can be no doubt that the report is against the interests of the farming community.
I do not think so.

I think it is, and the opinion of men just as well posted as the hon. minister is that the report is not a fair one. The investigation should not stop where it is, but further inquiry should be made to determine whether these men were mistaken or not. I am not casting any reflection on the officers of the department, but I do not know that a chemist is the best man to determine that particular thing. A practical farmer could investigate a matter of that kind just as well as a chemist. I do not see where chemical knowledge is required in such a matter. Mr. Shutt may be an excellent chemist, but I am not aware that his chemical knowledge would fit him better for a question of this kind than that of a man who is every day engaged in the feeding of hogs and the work of a farm generally. No doubt these are men well qualified to discharge technical duties, but I cannot see that because this opinion has been given by a chemist, it should have any more weight than if given by a butcher

I remember very well reading this bulletin and I very well remember Professor Shutt appearing before our committee to illustrate by a bulletin the results of feeding different foods to hogs. I consider it an extremely interesting report, but perhaps I might agree with some of what is said by hon. gentlemen opposite. Possibly the experiment might be carried still further. The bulletin did certainly show that corn was the most excellent feed for hogs. That is the general result of the experiment, as I remember. I suppose that probably the best food for hogs is peas, as shown by the results, and one of the poorest foods is corn. It so happens that the western part of the country grows a great deal of corn and feeds a great deal to hogs, so that nearly all the hogs from that section are practically corn-fed. Of course, I make that statement, not from personal knowledge, but because large quantities of corn are grown in that section, and I presume it is fed to the hogs. The Industry is one we cannot afford to lose. It is probably one of the most profitable branches of farming to-day, and if the results are such as were shown, it means to some extent some reflection on the hogs produced in the corn belt. Therefore it might be as well for the department to consider the carrying on of the experiment still further. In the section I come from, our farmers feed largely peas and oats to their hogs, and our hogs are noted as being first class. I have seen in the local papers complaints from the packers that corn-fed hogs were not as good as hogs fed on other food. Experiments were made and the animals were slaughtered and inspected and put through a process of chemical analysis, but that might not be sufficient to prove that corn was not as good feed for hogs, and under the circumstances I think possibly that the request of the hon. member for Bothwell is fair and reasonable and the experiment might be carried still further.

I was a little surprised at the curt manner in which the hon. Minister of Agriculture dealt with this question. I am not aware that he occupies a position which exempts him from replying to fair inquiries or that it is much to his credit to inform us, as he did, in a supercillious way, that he knows nothing About the reports in his own department. But he asserted very strongly that this report did not contain any such insinuation as I have stated. Well, let me read from the evidence given by Mr. Shutt in relation to the particular case to which I referred a moment ago. On page 124 of the report of the Select Standing Committee on Agriculture and Colonization, Mr. Shutt was asked by myself, with respect to the hogs that were slaughtered for experiment at the slaughter houses of Mr. Matthews in the city of Ottawa.

Q. Then why did you assume in this case, that the mothers were fed on corn, to put it in your report ?
A. I do not think I made that statement.
Q. You made it.
A. I made a scientific conjecture, nothing more. I say that the unweaned animals, the young animals, may be affected by the milk of their mother, and X see no reason to hesitate to further say that supposing the mother be fed largely on corn, she having been brought up on corn, the fat of her milk would have a tendency to make flesh, or rather the fat of her young, soft.
Q. Have you made a test to show if that is true ?
A. No.
Q. Where did you purchase them ?
A. In Essex and Kent. I cannot give you the names of the parties from whom they were bought.
Q. I do not want that. That being the case, up to that stage they could not have been fed upon corn much, could they ?
A. No.
Q. Did you wish to give the impression that by the mere fact their mothers were fed upon corn that they were soft.
A. I did not state that as a fact, but I said that it was significant that these pigs were the softest two of the four young pigs examined. I think it is probable-it is quite possible, at any rate, that if the mothers were largely corn fed. the milk would at	outset give that
character to the flesh of fheir young. I infer that such wmuld be the case. In the light of our subsequent work I felt justified in saying so.
Q. Quite so ; have you any evidence that all the pigs in Western Canada are fed on corn ?
A. Oh. no. I have never said they were.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is not necessary to read further to show that this gentleman came here and stated that this was a mere scientific conjecture, and from that, a report is sent out broadcast throughout this country as the hon. gentleman has stated, that contains on every page a condemnation which has no better ground than the statement of Professor Shutt on that occasion. That was an examination of which the hon. minister should have some knowledge. I am surprised that he does not know what is going, on in his own department, that he does not read the report of the committee respecting the department over which he presides and knows nothing of the evidence given before it, but must come here with the confession that he has not read the report and knows nothing of what is in it, knows nothing of the effect in the country of the evidence which his officers are sending out. And, yet, he lies back and, in an injured tone, refuses to answer questions. Now, may I be permitted to ask, with great humility, if he is disposed to let that libel stand uncontradicted without further evidence ?

In the first place, I doi not know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) has quoted me quite correctly. I did not say that I knew nothing of what occurred in the committee.

1 said that I could not remember the particular question that he referred to. I think I know something of what is going on in the committee and of the evidence given by my officers, but I confess that I do not carry all the details in my mind so as to be able to refer offdiand to any point which the hon. gentleman may happen to mention. He asks me if this evidence ought to be allowed to remain without further investigation. I confess that, up to the present, I have believed-and I have not yet seen reason to change my mind-that the conclusions of that report were fair and just on the whole. I did not draw from the conclusions as I remember then) the inference which the hon. gentleman seems to have drawn, that those conclusions were an imputation against the pigs of a certain place in Canada; but I did draw from the inference that pigs fed almost entirely upon corn were more likely to be soft in their flesh, than pigs fed in another way.

What led the hon. gentleman to that conclusion ?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE The facts in the report.
But, if the hon. gentleman will permit me, his own officer declares that that is a mere ' scientific conjecture.'

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) has quoted one particular phrase used in describing the results of experiments covering several hundred pigs and many different investigations. I confess I do not know just what Professor Shutt meant by the words ' scientific conjecture ' but they apply to one particular incident, one of many parts of the evidence, which evidence tended on the whole to the conclusions drawn In that report.

I do not wish to disturb the hon. gentleman, but the hon. gentleman will remember, perhaps, from reading the report from his own department that these questions were on special incidents given in the report we are discussing. Examples were given of tests made without locating the quarter from which the pigs came. But this incident was selected, and Professor Shutt said he did not know what the mothers were fed upon, that this was a mere scientific conjecture on his own part.

I cannot say if that was the case, because I do not remember the surroundings of the incident. But I do know that the conclusions were based upon the whole series of experiments. I think they extended over two years' work. All these pigs were bought as soon as they were weaned and brought here to be fed. That was the principle of the experiment. Some of these young pigs were slaughtered when they were first
brought here, to learn the condition of their flesh. Others were experimented on in feeding, and animals were slaughtered at different stages and their flesh subjected to examination. The hon. member for Haiton (Mr. Henderson) said he did not think the chemist the right man to do this kind of work. The chemist did only one part of the work. The animals were fed by the men in charge of them, and were slaughtered by the pork packers of Ottawa, who gave reports "from their practical standpoint as to the character of the flesh. The chemist came after and chemically analyzed the flesh of every pig and different parts of the carcass of every pig. One of the points we wished to arrive at was to know in what chemically soft pork consisted. The trade could tell us that such and such a pig was soft or such and such a side was soft. We wished to know the chemical characteristics of soft and hard pork. That is the reason the chemists took part in the experiment. And as he was the officer who took part In the whole thing, he made up the report and worked out the conclusions, based partly on his own work in the laboratory and partly on the reports of the other men engaged in the experiment. I confess that up to this moment I considered that the public at large, including hon. gentlemen opposite, had accepted that report as a final conclusion upon the subject. I want to say that as a result of that report and the information that was given by the series of experiments during the last two years, I think there has been much less salt pork in Canada than there was for the ten years preceding. I hear very few complaints on the part of packers of salt pork. I do not mean to say it is all due to the experiment; but I do believe that the result of that experiment gave information to the feeders of pork in this country which enabled them to a certain extent to have less risk in making salt pork, because it showed the food that seemed to be the best to make hard, and it showed some food which seemed to be objectionable for that purpose. If I find that the public wish further information, we should certainly inaugurate another series of experiments.

If the hon. gentleman had carefully read the evidence that was given by Mr. Shutt he would find that the chemical experiments have been thoroughly unreliable. I have no hesitation in making that statement in this House. What did we elicit in Mr. Shutt's examination ? For instance, he was asked if, when he made the statement in his report comparing pigs bought in the west and those bought in the east, they were all alike, or was there some cause from which salt pork was found in the same condition in both lots, and he answered that was the, case. If that is the case, how can you lay down any rule? It is dangerous for any one to set afloat statements upon mere scientific bubble-blowing. With

regard to the chemical experiments, I have pointed out the contradictory sections of that bulletin with regard to the oil test, as it is called, the temperatures and so on, where the temperatures were professedly the same and he got very different results. I make no apology for saying that it is a most unreliable and damaging report. There is no difference in the feeding conditions. People are not so stupid in the west, although they live in a corn belt where pigs are fed entirely upon corn, as not to know the*value of feeding mixed grains other than corn. It was unfair to assume that because a lot of pigs were bought in the west, they were fed on com any more than in the east. The farmers in the west understand as well as those in the east that it is to their interest to feed pigs upon mixed grains.
